text:
My 3-Week Solo Travel in Spain: Hiking Camino Primitivo, Viewing Solar Eclipse & Touring Old Cities

How is it possible to describe in words a hodgepodge of feelings, sentiments, and inspirations, some even contradictory, about all that I learned from trekking Camino Primitivo and solo travel in Spain?
Perhaps this famous short poem is the way to start:

Traveler, There Is No Road
(“Caminante, no hay camino”) by Antonio Machado

Traveler, your footprints
are the only road, nothing else.

Traveler, there is no road;
you make your own path as you walk.

As you walk, you make your own road,
and when you look back
you see the path
you will never travel again.

Traveler, there is no road;
only a ship’s wake on the sea.

(translated by Mary G. Berg and Dennis Maloney)

I went to Spain by myself, not knowing Spanish, and spent three weeks there traveling from place to place almost daily.

I trekked for 15 days (with Day 10 as a rest day), around 200 miles (310 kilometers), up and down the Asturian mountains from Oviedo to Santiago de Compostela. Camino Primitivo is considered one of the hardest Camino routes, but also one of the most scenic.

– To watch this as a 17-minute video, with photos
https://t.co/bmPoTD6Xtj

– To listen to this as a 17-minute podcast
https://t.co/dW4W2bW92c

I visited five old Spanish cities (Madrid, Leon, Segovia, Toledo, Alcala de Henares) on my own before and after hiking Camino Primitivo, in addition to the three cities on my Camino: Oviedo, Lugo, and Santiago.

I came back with more wisdom, peace, endurance, independence, tolerance, humility, willpower, and goal-oriented determination.

Before embarking on the Camino, I spent three days in Madrid’s art museums. After Santiago, I went to Leon by myself to visit the city and see the full solar eclipse. Then I traveled to Segovia, Toledo, and Alcala de Henares before flying back from Madrid to SFO.

Walking about 15 miles a day for two weeks in the peaceful Spanish countryside slowed down the digital speed of life, and made me more conscious of slowing down and being deliberate. Trekking in the misty mornings through villages and rural landscapes instilled its quiet maturity in me. I recently developed a liking for economy of words, and for slowness in action and judgment.

The three-week adventure was also a photographic feast: I took thousands of photos, some of them spectacular. I will process, edit, and upload them later to my photography website.

Though by myself, I was never alone, and never felt lonely. God prepared everything I needed  before I even realized that I would need it: from a Spanish teacher on the airplane who was going on the same Camino at the same time, to the Bulgarian herb candies gifted to me by a fellow peregrina (pilgrim), a Bulgarian mother who also hiked the Primitivo with her 18-year-old son. A few days later, these herb candies were the perfect cough drops after I caught a cold virus from a hotel’s AC in Leon.

In fact, the best times were those when I was by myself, conversing one on one with God, thanking Him for the awesome mountain views and the people He placed on my journey, and asking Him for guidance. When I was hiking solo, I could allow inspirations to arrive on their terms, I could think, reflect, and admire nature and old buildings without the need to listen to others.

I love local Spanish cuisines and the Spanish people.  I was helped so many times by their genuine kindness everywhere and whenever I needed it. God put the right people in my path at the right time, and taught me to trust myself.

He also placed them in my care. Personally, an accomplishment more significant than hiking the Camino itself was that I kept my promise to God and to the hiking partner He put in my care, and endured till the end.  After all, it is a pilgrimage on which I literally walked the talk.

I found that the most challenging part was neither language-related (thanks to Google Translate) nor physical, but psychological and relational, in dealing with my own primordial fears and with my hiking partner.  If I were ever to do another Camino (not Primitivo again) in the future, unless I am blessed with a mutually compatible hiking companion whom I know well, I would rather do it by myself without being tethered to anyone, speaking Spanish or not.

The continuous trekking, day after day, added stress and pain to my knee and ankle. Seeing me limping in pain, a French woman I met on the Camino and hiked with for a day gave me her pain relief cream, even though she might have needed it.

I felt the best of humanity from the pure kindness of others without any strings attached, without any expectations for reciprocity: from a Spanish mother and her daughter who offered help with Spanish language without being asked, and from the good-natured, hospitable group of Spaniards with whom I shared the same hostel room.

I also experienced the not-so-good part of humanity, which taught me to accept people where they are, the way they are, however different or even wrong. Sometimes the way to deal with it was to ignore, to confront, or to respond with tacit understanding. Forgiveness and letting go, when practiced, remove all undue weight and obstacles.

The Asturian mountains were beautiful, but not comparable to the awesome mountains and magnificent landscapes in the western US. Even though I could sleep in a bed and take a shower at each albergue (hostel), I still prefer the total wilderness experience of hiking and camping in the high country of Yosemite or other national parks in the US. If walking the Camino was a spiritual journey (it is also a mental and physical endurance test), I boil down my Christian faith to two words: forgive and repent. Without these, there is no way to reach love, peace, and joy.

Not being a Catholic, arriving at Santiago de Compostela was more symbolic and metaphoric. Santiago is a goal. Life revolves around goals. I am now better prepared for my next career goals. Climbing many mountains and hills on the Camino Primitivo has given me a focused, single-minded approach.

I returned with more calmness and a new mental habit of minimizing my response to stress triggers (though not successful every time.)  I gained a detached way of approaching challenges in life.

This budding, unfazed and unfrazzled approach resulted cumulatively from dealing with a number of challenges. These included dealing with an unavailable Renfe train (Renfe is Spain’s national railway operator), the last-minute dash to the airport to get the last seat on a flight to Oviedo, the changing dynamics with my hiking partner, and problem-solving in unexpected situations. Sometimes I relied on others’ help, sometimes I resorted to a combination of intuition, judgement, and resourcefulness of my own.

Among so many things I have learned, here are a few that stood out:

Trust my own instinct
It is harder to trust and follow my own instinct, which, in my opinion, is one way God sends me messages. It takes focus and practice to tune out external noises, temptations, self-doubt, and distractions that override my own instinct.  Every time I ignored what my instinct told me, I suffered the consequences: Had I listened to my better judgment not to turn on the AC and thus not needed to use the hotel’s blanket, I might have avoided the viral cold I believed came from the AC’s contaminated filter and the bed bugs from the hotel blanket.

Every time I heeded my instinct, things turned out right: not listening to a Renfe employee’s wrong advice and finding the correct direction to the right cercania (commuter train) by seeking a second opinion from the ticket office; not following the crowd on the wrong path on the Camino, etc.

Adventure solo or with others
Many men and women chose to walk the Camino Primitivo solo. A lot of them were going through transitions in life. Some were going to start a new career, taking several weeks off between jobs to walk the Camino. Some quit their jobs and were in search of themselves. On Primitivo, most were in their 30s, 40s, or 50s. Many were teachers. It makes sense since they have long summer vacations when schools are closed.

On the more popular Camino Francés, there were younger crowds in their 20’s.

Most non-solo pilgrims walking together were couples in stable relationships or were related by blood. I saw families: an entire nuclear family, mother and daughter, mother and son, sisters, brothers, father with adult children in their 20s.

Other than families and loved ones, sharing the journey with someone you just met on the Camino usually is not meant for the entire journey. Maybe just a day or two, in hindsight. A couple of days walking, eating, and sharing a hostel room together can reveal a lot about what kind of person we each are.

To me, to keep my Camino as my own experience required intentionality about independence, given the human needs for both community and solitude.

Solitude and companionship; detachment and community
Solitude is far more enjoyable than companionship formed out of convenience. (A completely unfit companion could ruin an adventure experience, as I learned from a previous wilderness backpacking trip in Yosemite.)

Even if the companionship was out of convenience or mutual practical needs, I could still have found solitude by creating my own internal space, sometimes walking alone on the Camino. To make the Camino my own demands a balance between community and self, the need to be social as well as being independent and detached.  I wish I hadn’t exerted myself to keep up with the pace of my hiking companion.

A companionship is not enjoyable if it is mainly out of fear (fear of being alone, fear of abandonment, fear of not belonging, etc.), or out of need. Whom I travel with is just as important as where I travel, just like growing a business with a partner. Again, it is better to do it solo than with an unfit partner. Having a great hiking partner can add so much more joy to an adventure. That would be the best.

Human minds are inclined to remember the hurt more than the good. Life is too short. Let the bad rapidly recede in the river of memories. Choose to remember the good memories, forgive others’ frailties, and forgive mine too.

Some encounters are meant for a specific purpose. Once it is over, it is over.
None of the encounters with fellow pilgrims were planned or plannable. In each case I learned something from each person, and then we each moved on. Perhaps that was the beauty of it. No attachment, no expectation, no duty, yet the connection was real. We all have left something with each other: ourselves.

All experiences in life share this passing nature.  Passing by every place, every person, and passing through every day, like a dream. You cannot step into the same river of life twice.  Each passing moment: let it pass.

Home, sweet home: At the end of every day of trekking, I shared some photos and a brief message with my sons and those in their lives. That connection to the home base anchored my vagabond journey from one new place to another in a foreign country.  Towards the end of my third week of Spain tours, the longing for home increased its volume like Maurice Ravel’s Boléro. The Odyssey theme of the pull and push between adventure and going home was felt more intensely as the sojourn extended.

Is the Camino for everyone? I am not sure.  It is a unique lifestyle experience. My lesson is that if you can handle both solitude and community, or if you prefer to be left alone, or if you have good companionship, you can enjoy it and learn about yourself and about life on the Camino.

To me, it was a worthy growth experience, mentally, physically, and spiritually.  The natural scenery and historical sites I passed through are best accessed, visited, and enjoyed by hiking. Walking many hours, mostly in nature and through villages, day after day, is meditative.

The restorative effect of walking in nature, day after day, connects us to the celestial rhythm of Mother Earth, which is therapeutic and healing.

Some people intentionally bring their unresolved issues to the Camino and seek resolutions or closures through walking long miles. Some choose to be open to whatever inspiration comes randomly.  I did both and got both.

The Camino is a meeting place of all nationalities. I met people from France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, the UK, Serbia and Montenegro, Bulgaria, Italy, Hungary, Korea, Hong Kong, Australia, the United States, and of course, España.

Another unexpected good thing from hiking the Camino was that I came home five pounds lighter.  I came home with my Camino habit of rising before dawn, starting the day while it is dark and having an unhurried, quiet morning. I had wanted to do this for so long but never could consistently get up early. Thanks to Spain’s fierce summer sun and hot weather in July and August, I and my hiking companion got up around 5:30 a.m. We hit the trail with my headlamp around 6 a.m. when it was still dark. We did most of the walking during the cool hours in the morning, and wrapped up seven hours of hiking around 1 p.m.

Even though I did not think it was a big deal when I reached Santiago, looking back now, I am so grateful that I did not get sick or injured during the Camino, and completed the journey exactly as scheduled. I realize that I accomplished quite a bit over three weeks, including touring Spain before and after the Camino. This trip has changed me.

I look forward to more adventures in other parts of the world.

This is only a short summary of my three-week adventure in Spain in the summer of 2026.  I will get around to writing more details later.

text:
If you live in California, New York, Arizona, Washington, Oregon or Nevada, do not try to flip your first house

Not "it's harder." The math does not close. Here's the math:

A first flip needs $30,000 of profit on paper before you buy. One surprise behind a wall eats $10,000-$15,000. One extra month of holding eats another $2,000-$5,000. Under $30,000 you aren't investing, you're gambling with a paint roller

Ohio version:

Buy: $95,000
Renovate: $25,000
Worth fixed: $160,000
Hard money covers 80% of the purchase and all of the reno. You bring about $19,000 plus closing
6-week renovation. Sell it, or refinance and rent it to a Section 8 tenant for $1,375 a month
Profit on paper: $40,000
Your money exposed: about $23,000

California version, same ugly starter house:

The rough house is $550,000. Fixed up, call it $650,000. Labor costs more, so the same renovation is $60,000
The 70% rule says your max offer is $650,000 × 0.70 − $60,000 = $395,000
Nobody in California sells that house for $395,000. So you pay the $550,000
You bring $110,000 down. Hard money on that loan runs roughly $4,000-$5,000 a month while you work
Sell at $650,000, pay a 5% commission ($32,500), closing costs both directions, 4 months of holding
Profit on paper: negative. You did 4 months of work to lose about $15,000 with $110,000 of your own money exposed the entire time

Same 27-year-old. Same skill. Same Sherwin-Williams paint. The only variable is the zip code

The states where a first flip actually closes: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Wisconsin, West Virginia, Georgia, Alabama, Florida, Texas. The Carolinas if you're going Section 8

"I'm not moving to Ohio"

You don't have to. I buy houses in 4 states and I've never stood inside most of them. Pick a market where the math works, hire a contractor and an inspector who live there, buy off Zillow. Your first house should be wherever $23,000 turns into $40,000, not wherever you sleep

The people who flip successfully in expensive states already had money. The people who start with $23,000 start where $23,000 is enough

And the $23,000 doesn't have to be yours. You can access up to $250K in 0% interest money to fund your first flip. Link in my bio, fill out the form and I'll hit you back

text:
We have sucked for the past 5 seasons and we haven't had a 10-win team in almost a decade. I remember hearing about how we lost to Bama 9 years in a row between PBP and BOTT, and we're fast approaching that now. It's really been the roughest stretch for Auburn football in not only my lifetime, but the lifetime of pretty much anyone under 75. 

I don't want to be too down about it. There's plenty to be optimistic about with Golesh. But at least I can go into this season not worried sick about having high expectations - from myself or others. I can hope for the best without being that unrealistic Barner either. There is some peace in that. 

I also think the overall changing landscape of college athletics is making it harder to be emotionally involved. I don't know the names of many people on our team. And it's starting to feel like that every year. I spent a lot of time last year studying our roster just to watch us piss away 7 very winnable games. And I watched a lot of people who chose Auburn really just chose a slightly higher offer for this season - not the many things that make Auburn special. I wish them well, but now we start over with new people. 

All that said, I'm sure once kickoff happens tomorrow, I'll put all that cynicism aside and go back to letting 18-22 year old dudes determine the course of my mental health for the next several months. The way it should be. 

And hopefully we'll surprise myself and others. I think there's a lot to like about Alex Golesh. I've never called it a home run hire, but at least it's a guy we all tend to like. For now anyway, and hopefully for a long time. 

I just want to feel things again. Maybe this can be the year. But alas, maybe not. 

My prediction: 7-5. Even though 7-5 used to be a down year for us overall, it would actually be marked improvement this year, and I would take it. I imagine we'll have some close losses, but I doubt we absolutely snatch defeat from the jaws of victory the way we were the last 3 seasons. Anything over .500 is a respectable year 1. Finding a way to go 8-4 would be a success.

text:
Of course I had to try employing Open AI's new flagship Model Astra to handicap the races in Australia today plugged into the MWP database! 

Here is what it had to say - one thing to note is that it does not know about the odds, just a read on available data and Expected Rating model-predictions (like what you would see if you study the form yourself at Mr. World Pool): 

Interesting races on Saturday, 5 September 2026

This is a starting point for handicapping, not a list of betting instructions. The model's expected performance at today's weights starts the discussion; recent performances, repeatability, conditions and race shape can change the reading. A narrow first place is not a standout.

Going is the current description in the form, not a guarantee of Saturday's conditions. Confirm final runners and conditions before using the preview. 

Where I would spend the time:

Sandown Hillside R7 | EVAPORATE: an encouraging return after doing early work. PINSTRIPED makes the comparison interesting through both his finish and today's weights. 

Eagle Farm R8 | SER JOH versus BRINDAVAN: a recent head-to-head, different runs through the race, and a change in relative weights. 

Royal Randwick R7 | PRIVATE EYE: current Group-level form behind a model lead; IDLE FLYER is the improving alternative whose finishing position undersells her performance. 

Sandown Hillside R8 | CAVALRY GIRL versus GIGA KICK: repeatable current speed against an established higher ceiling. NATURAL FLING complicates the pace. 

Royal Randwick R9 | CEOLWULF has the stronger recent return; FANGIRL remains close enough on the projections to matter. 

Sandown Hillside

About Sandown Hillside: a left-handed, galloping course with an uphill, medium-long finishing straight. There is room to finish, but horses still have to settle and conserve enough to use it.

R7 — So You Think Stakes, 7½f

EVAPORATE is one of the sounder starting points on the Australian cards. His return at Caulfield was more interesting than a routine third: after being a little slow away he worked around the field to lead, then was only headed late. That is a credible recent performance to bring into this assignment, and the model gives him meaningful separation.

PINSTRIPED prevents this becoming a one-horse paragraph. He finished directly behind Evaporate in that race after needing room, and now receives weight from him rather than meeting him level. His recent efforts are strong enough to make that change matter. FREEDOM RALLY adds a different positive: a decisive win over this very course and distance last time, albeit on heavy ground.

The read: Evaporate leads the assessment, but Pinstriped is the counterargument to examine closely. The case is current form and a suitable assignment, not simply the highest number.

R8 — Moir Stakes, G1, 5f

GIGA KICK is narrowly ahead on the projections, not in a different race. His best established sprint form is formidable, but he returns from a break and his outstanding autumn effort was over further.

CAVALRY GIRL is the more immediate form story. Three straight wins; more importantly, the last two performances were at a similar high level. She also won over this course and distance despite waiting for a gap. That is more persuasive than a single sudden spike followed by an assumption that improvement continues forever.

The questions are real: this is stronger opposition, and those recent wins came on soft or heavy ground. Nor should an easy lead be written into the case. NATURAL FLING has shown plenty of early speed herself and gets substantial weight relief, although she is far less exposed against older sprinters.

The read: Cavalry Girl has a serious case beside the established star. This is a competitive sprint, not a licence for maximum confidence.

R9 — Chautauqua Stakes, G3, 6½f

TENNESSEE BOUND's six wins from seven starts and favourable weight position make him the model's starting point. But his first defeat was not an obvious hard-luck story: he followed the winner with clear running and could not match him. His earlier wins were stronger performances, so the question is whether he returns to that level.

WARNIE supplies the argument that the shortlist must not lose. He was fourth at Caulfield after settling a long way back, then finished strongly. The performance itself was better than the placing suggests and makes him a proper winning contender if reproduced here. Sandown gives that finish room, provided the early race is run to suit.

The read: Tennessee Bound's overall profile versus Warnie's more compelling latest effort. Both deserve an argument, not just a rank.

Rest of the card

R2 | 1 mile | BLUE WILLOW has proven Hillside mile form, but her latest run was below that level. CELESTIAL ZARA arrives off two wins and a much less exposed profile; a stronger mile test is the next question. 

R3 | 5f | BEHAVIOUR heads a close model group. MAINMANKASH's emphatic Sale win would make him a serious threat if repeated, but it came on heavy ground; Behaviour beat him the start before. An interesting rematch, not a clear selection. 

R4 | 6½f | FUNDAMENTAL NATURE returned with a win; CRUISERWEIGHT has won two of only three starts and draws inside. Progress versus progress, with NIC'S CHOICE another whose best recent effort would matter. 

R10 | 1 mile | MR VERSE leads narrowly. CHANGING COLOURS has consecutive wins supported by similar performances; STAY SILENT has won three straight. Several current profiles, limited separation.

R1, R5 and R6 were excluded by the insufficient-data filter. The full Sandown Hillside card is listed as published on Mr. World Pool.

Australia — Eagle Farm

About Eagle Farm: a right-handed course with sweeping bends and a medium-long straight. The current going is soft. 

R8 — Open handicap, 7f

SER JOH and BRINDAVAN make this the best handicapping puzzle on the card. Brindavan won their latest meeting; Ser Joh was second after being held up until late, then finished soundly once clear. They do not need invented excuses to make the rematch interesting.

There is a tangible change: Ser Joh received one kilo from Brindavan that day and receives three here. The model only narrowly prefers him, but the combination of the interrupted run and the improved relative weights gives the preference substance.

Brindavan remains a serious opponent. He finished off strongly to win on his return and may come forward himself. Both draw inside; a smooth passage is an opportunity, not a promise. Ser Joh's preceding second also came after he had been allowed to dictate, so he is not a horse to excuse automatically every time he gets beaten.

The read: a useful Ser Joh case, with the winner of the last meeting fully respected. Modest model separation, much richer racing context.

R6 — Benchmark 70, 7½f

PRECISE STAR has built his sequence rather than merely collected three wins. His performances have improved through the preparation, and the last win at Ipswich was emphatic. The inside draw offers options, and he leads the model without being far clear.

The caveat is how that last success happened: he controlled the race and kicked away. A stronger metropolitan contest does not guarantee the same comfort. RIEZ SOUVENT and DETRIMENTAL are close enough on the projections that he needs to bring his progress with him.

The read: a progressive horse worth following through the class test, not an assumption that the last winning margin repeats.

R3 — Benchmark 78, 12f

CAPTAIN MAVERICK and TRAPALANDA are virtually inseparable on the model. But CHILLAXING should be central to the human reading: he beat Captain Maverick over this course and distance on soft ground, and their relative weights do not turn that result in Captain Maverick's favour.

Captain Maverick has been consistently competitive, but his recent notes describe favourable runs rather than repeated misfortune. Chillaxing has delivered the win at today's trip. This is a good example of why the nominal model leader is an opening question, not the finished argument.

Rest of the card

R1 | 5f | ESHA brings a recent course-and-distance win. FORGOTTEN SPIRIT finished ahead of her here on soft earlier in the preparation. One runner lacks a usable history in the available form, limiting confidence in a full-field ranking. 

R2 | 5f | FLEETWOOD, ZOUBABY and BIANCELLI sit in a tightly packed group. There is not enough separation to make a strong case from the rankings alone.

R4 | 6f | RHETORIC and THATS ARCHIES GIRL lead a close field. Lower priority: no strong combined case emerged.

R5 | 9f | LUTON HOO, MIRRA IMPACT and ROCK HARD LOVE are closely matched. Rock Hard Love brings a recent win, but this is a competitive assessment rather than a standout.

R7 | 7f | SHELSTEIN's recent win and light weight put him in the conversation with MISTER BIANCO and FUKUBANA. Small field, but still little model separation. 

R9 | 6f | STORMLAND, MANPOWER and FIRE BOMBER all bring current competitive form. Manpower has the recent winning result; the others have been knocking on the door. 

R10 | 6f | KING KAPA and CASPERNOVA bring relevant recent efforts. Large differences in assigned weights make the declared weights important to check; no strong single-horse conclusion.

Australia — Royal Randwick

About Royal Randwick: a right-handed, galloping course with a medium-long finishing straight. Its finish asks horses to sustain a run. Several major contenders are returning for spring, so readiness today and longer-term ability should not be treated as the same thing. 

R7 — Tramway Stakes, G2, 7f

PRIVATE EYE has one of the more coherent cases on the card. His recent second at Caulfield was a strong performance at the right trip, following competitive Group 1 runs in Queensland. He is not relying solely on an old career peak. The model puts him first, with a meaningful but not overwhelming advantage.

IDLE FLYER's sixth on her return is worth reading past. She finished without threatening, but the performance was better than her earlier winning figures. Second-up, with a favourable draw and less weight than Private Eye, she has a credible route into the race without needing a fabricated hard-luck story.

HEADLEY GRANGE has already shown a level capable of winning this, notably in his Queensland Group 1 success. He returns from a break after a weaker run, so the ceiling is there but its immediate availability is less certain.

The read: Private Eye is the sound starting point; Idle Flyer is the improving profile to keep beside him.

R8 — Concorde Stakes, G2, 5f

TEMPTED has the model's narrow preference and a strong winning record at Randwick. Her last three wins were backed by consistently high performances. That gives the return substance, but most of the recent evidence is over further and she has not raced since April.

ROSELYN'S STAR is the latest-performance challenge to the model ordering. His Rosehill win was strong enough to put him into the winning discussion if reproduced. It was on heavy ground over a slightly longer trip, however, so copying the number straight across would skip the actual handicapping.

HEADWALL brings another serious ceiling and won here over this trip on his last appearance, but that was a year ago. Respect the targeted spring context without declaring a long absence irrelevant. STEADY READY is also worth locating on the pace map.

The read: Tempted deserves the lead paragraph, not a claim that the others cannot match her. Readiness and the conditions under which each horse produced its best matter greatly.

R9 — Chelmsford Stakes, G2, 1 mile

CEOLWULF and FANGIRL form the model's top pair. Ceolwulf's return over 7f was the stronger recent effort: he kept finding towards the line and now moves back to the mile. That is a more concrete positive than simply expecting a famous horse to improve second-up.

Fangirl was left with plenty to do on her return and did not get into contention. It was not an obstructed run home, so the case should be fitness and recovery of her established level, not traffic that was never there. She remains close on the forecast and is not eliminated by one disappointing result.

The read: preference to Ceolwulf on the latest evidence; confidence in the leading pair is stronger than confidence that only one can win.

Rest of the card

R1 | 7f | DUSTY BAY has a consistent current profile. SATNESS is close; FELIX MAJESTIC's last performance merits more attention than his model position alone.

R2 | 6f | WAYBURN and MRS GOLDBERG bring recent wins. LORD REMLAP is unbeaten but returns from a break. Several positives, with no overwhelming leader. 

R3 | 5½f | ERNAUX is fit and consistent, but PETTICOAT and AGATHA are close enough to make the model order a weak separator. 

R4 | 12f | THEBUDGIESMUGLA and SO YOU ARE are essentially a joint starting point. Both have relevant staying form; splitting them on a tiny forecast difference would be false precision. 

R5 | 6f | NIGHT AGENT leads narrowly but returns from a break. CLEAR PROOF's consecutive wins and strong latest performance make him a necessary addition to the discussion; ALABAMA STATE has current form too. 

R10 | 1 mile | STARZINTHEIREYES leads a close group, returning from a campaign over further. ISTOLEA MERC and WATSON have more recent runs behind them. Plenty depends on how the returning horse fits this shorter assignment.

R6 was excluded by the insufficient-data filter. The full Royal Randwick card is listed as published on Mr. World Pool.

Good luck.

Recovery is possible, and no one has to face it alone.

This month is National Recovery Month, and Sheriff Jonathon Horton and the Etowah County Sheriff's Office wants every resident to know that help is available right here in our community.

📞 SAMHSA National Helpline — 1-800-662-4357 (24/7, free, confidential)
📱 211 Alabama — a great first call for connecting with local mental health and substance use resources
💻 ConnectAL — Alabama's behavioral health treatment finder tool (https://t.co/VKehGA9nTH)

🏥 Local support close to home:
Cherokee/Etowah/DeKalb Mental Health Center — (256) 549-0807
NewLife for Women — Gadsden
BHG Gadsden Treatment Center — Gadsden

We're also proud to be part of the solution directly — our detention center now offers a Medication-Assisted Treatment program to help individuals in custody take real steps toward recovery.

Addiction affects families across every corner of our county, but recovery is possible, and support is closer than you think. If you or someone you love needs help, please reach out.

Weekend Agriculture
Publishing Date: September 5, 2026

As September opens across the nation's midsection, the 2026 row crop season is transitioning rapidly into early harvest mode. The USDA’s final August Crop Progress report confirmed that national corn condition ratings stabilized at 57% good/excellent, with 19% of the national crop now fully mature tracking three points ahead of the five-year average. Soybean conditions held steady at 60% good/excellent, with early leaf dropping reaching 13% as pod fill draws to a close across northern and western districts.

Grain and livestock boards closed the week with active position adjustments ahead of the Labor Day holiday weekend. Futures markets navigated two way trade as operators balanced pre-harvest hedging pressure against steady daily flash export sales to China and Latin American destinations. In the livestock complex, cattle futures held firm backed by steady cash trade in northern feedlots and tight market ready supplies, while lean hog values traded with minor holiday weekend adjustments.

USDA AND POLICY DIGEST

The grain trade spent the week reviewing the latest USDA Crop Progress update, which outlined rapid crop maturity across dry western growing zones:

National corn conditions held firm at 57% good to excellent. Maturity advanced to 19% nationwide, while 62% of the crop has reached the dent stage and 91% has cleared the dough stage. Initial high moisture corn cutting gathered momentum across southern portions of the Corn Belt.

Soybean condition ratings held unchanged at 60% good/excellent. Pod setting reached 94% complete, while leaf dropping advanced to 13%, signaling an early start to combine runs across early planted acres.

Spring wheat harvest made major headway across the Northern Plains, jumping to 69% complete nationally, while winter wheat producers began field preparation and initial drill setup for the 2027 crop.

On the policy and trade front, discussion across agricultural organizations focused on early fall rail logistics, Mississippi River water levels, and export terminal readiness ahead of peak harvest volume. Export reporting channels remained active into month end, with private exporters confirming continuous sales of new crop soybeans and corn to primary destination buyers.

WEATHER, SOIL AND FIELD REALITY

Weather conditions across the primary agricultural core featured late-summer warmth and scattered rain showers, allowing fields to dry down for combine access:

In the Western Corn Belt and Plains, warm, breezy conditions accelerated crop maturation across Nebraska, Kansas, and the Dakotas. Dryland fields that suffered under August thermal stress are drying rapidly, prompting growers to prepare storage bins and grain handling setups early.

In the Central and Eastern Corn Belt, states like Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana saw favorable late season conditions, with Iowa maintaining strong baseline ratings at 76% of its corn and 75% of its soybeans in good/excellent condition. Recent localized showers helped finish late planted soybeans without delaying early field work.

In the Delta and South, corn harvest reached advanced stages with producers reporting variable yield results based on summer irrigation availability, while early soybean cutting began on mature fields.

Across regional production zones:

In the Western Plains, operators focused on staging grain carts, inspecting elevator pits, and finalizing early corn delivery contracts.

In the Central Corn Belt, field managers conducted final pre-harvest stalk strength testing and lodging evaluations across high-yielding fields.

In the Northern Plains, custom harvest crews continued rapid progress through spring wheat and canola acres.

In the Southern Plains, pasture conditions remain tight, keeping livestock producers reliant on early supplemental hay feeding.

MARKET AND BOARD REVIEW

Board trading closed Friday with balanced positioning as traders squared accounts ahead of the holiday weekend and prepared for the upcoming September WASDE report.

Weekly commodity settlements closed around these core baselines:

December Corn Futures: Settled near $4.12 to $4.22 per bushel, balancing early harvest pressure against steady export demand and lower yield expectations in dry zones.

November Soybean Futures: Traded in the $10.15 to $10.40 per bushel range, underpinned by steady daily export flashes to China and solid domestic crush margins.

December Wheat Futures: Held steady near $5.40 to $5.60 per bushel as spring wheat harvest completion balanced global trade headlines.

WTI Crude Oil: Traded near $87 to $89 per barrel, sustaining elevated operational costs for harvest fuel, transport, and commercial crop drying.

Live Cattle Futures: CME October live cattle settled near $218.50 per hundredweight, backed by tight fed cattle inventories and steady cash bids.

Lean Hog Futures: October lean hog futures held near $80.50 per hundredweight on steady domestic pork demand.

Cash grain prices and interior basis across the Corn Belt reflected quiet country selling ahead of combine activity:

Corn Belt Cash Corn Bids: Country elevator bids posted between $3.95 and $4.25 per bushel, with interior country basis averaging 20 cents to 35 cents under the December contract. Ethanol processing facilities offered competitive local bids ranging from $4.30 to $4.45 per bushel.

Corn Belt Cash Soybean Bids: Interior elevator bids ranged from $9.60 to $10.10 per bushel, while major crushing mills held firm bids near $10.25 to $10.55 per bushel to lock in early harvest delivery commitments.

Corn Belt Cash Wheat Bids: Country bids across winter and spring wheat zones held between $5.50 and $6.20 per bushel, with basis holding steady on milling quality.

In livestock markets, Choice boxed beef cutouts maintained firm baseline pricing near $384.00 per hundredweight, while cash cattle trade held solid in Northern feedlots at $233.00 to $235.00 live, underpinned by light market-ready numbers.

TECHNICAL SPOTLIGHT, HISTORY AND HOMESTEAD

In agricultural technology, adoption of telematics driven grain cart scales and real time yield mapping systems expanded ahead of harvest. By automatically syncing weight data between combines, grain carts, and semi trucks, farm managers are streamlining field to elevator inventory tracking and eliminating manual scale ticket logging.

Looking back at historical milestones, early September marks the 1930s commercialization of portable farm grain augers. By replacing hand-shoveling at the bin site, powered augers revolutionized grain storage mechanics, enabling the rise of modern high capacity grain bins and farm scale handling systems across the Midwest.

On the homestead and in the field:

Fall Pasture Strategy: Smallholders prepared for cool-season grass recovery, resting key paddocks and applying early autumn nitrogen applications where moisture allowed.

Fix-It Corner: Pre-harvest machinery checks enter the final stretch inspect combine elevator chains, calibrate grain tank moisture sensors, service cart driveline U-joints, and check bin aeration fans before the first load arrives.

Producer Voice: "The corn dried down fast in this heat we're greasing the combine and making sure the augers are ready to roll right after the holiday."

St. Anger is the eighth studio album by American heavy metal band Metallica, released on June 5, 2003, through Elektra Records in the United States and Vertigo Records elsewhere. It was the last Metallica album released through Elektra and the final collaboration between Metallica and longtime producer Bob Rock, with whom the band had worked since 1990. This is also Metallica's only album without an official bassist, as Jason Newsted left the band prior to the recording sessions. Rock played in Newsted's place, while Robert Trujillo joined the band following its completion. Although he does not play on the album, Trujillo is listed as a member in the liner notes and appears in photos with the band in the album's booklet.

Recording began in April 2001 but was postponed after rhythm guitarist and vocalist James Hetfield entered rehabilitation for alcoholism and various other addictions, and did not resume until May 2002. The recording is the subject of the 2004 documentary film Metallica: Some Kind of Monster. St. Anger departed from Metallica's signature style with an alternative metal style, raw production, metallic drum sound, and devoid of their usual guitar solos. The artwork was created by frequent Metallica collaborator Pushead.

St. Anger was intended for release on June 10, 2003, but was released five days earlier due to concerns over unlicensed distribution via peer-to-peer file sharing networks. Despite mixed reviews, it debuted at the top of sales charts in 14 countries, including the US Billboard 200. Metallica spent two years touring to promote the album. In 2004, the lead single, "St. Anger", won a Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance. St. Anger was certified double platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) for shipping two million copies in the US; it has sold nearly six million copies worldwide.

Recording and musical style
After the departure of Jason Newsted (left) in 2001, Robert Trujillo became Metallica's new bassist in February 2003 and toured with the band in support of St. Anger.
Further information: Metallica: Some Kind of Monster
Metallica rented an old United States Army barracks on the Presidio of San Francisco, and converted it into a makeshift studio in January 2001.[1] As plans were being made to begin writing and recording their first album in nearly five years, the band postponed the recording because of bassist Jason Newsted's departure from Metallica on January 17, 2001, with Newsted stating his departure was due to "private and personal reasons and the physical damage I have done to myself over the years while playing the music that I love".[2] Due to the difficulty in immediately finding or auditioning for a replacement for Newsted to write and record with so close to the rescheduled sessions, Metallica accepted an offer from Bob Rock to play bass on the album in Newsted's place, and stated they would find an official bass player upon the album's completion.[1] In February 2003, as St. Anger was nearing completion, Metallica hired Robert Trujillo as their new bassist. He appeared on the footage of studio rehearsals of St. Anger in its entirety, which was included on DVD in the album package.[1]

In July 2001, recording came to a halt when James Hetfield entered rehab for alcoholism and other undisclosed addictions.[3] Hetfield returned to the band in December 2001,[4] but was only allowed to work on the album from noon to 4:00 PM as the band resumed recording on April 12, 2002. Due to his personal problems, as well as Metallica's internal struggles, the band hired a personal enhancement coach, Phil Towle. This, and the recording of the album, was documented by filmmakers Joe Berlinger and Bruce Sinofsky and released in 2004 as the film Metallica: Some Kind of Monster.[5] Metallica abandoned their Presidio studio and instead recorded at a new studio in San RAFAEL, California, known as "HQ", from May 2002 until April 2003.[6] 15 tracks from the Presidio sessions were ultimately unused.[7]

When denied a license to teach because he was only qualified for religious instruction, he earned a second doctorate in history from the Sorbonne in Paris.[5] With this he secured his teaching license and was able to provide religious instruction. AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

KENITES.
By: Emil G. Hirsch, Bernhard Pick, George A. Barton
—Biblical Data:
A tribe of Palestine, mentioned in the time of Abraham as possessing a part of the promised land (Gen. xv. 19). At the Exodus it inhabited the vicinity of Sinai and Horeb; and to it belonged Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses (Judges i. 16). In Ex. iii. 1 Jethro is said to have been "priest of Midian" and a Midianite (Num. iv. 29); hence the conclusion seems justified that the Midianites and Kenites are identical. The Kenites journeyed with the Israelites to Palestine (Judges i. 16); and their encampment, apart from the latter's, was noticed by Balaam (Num. xxiv. 21-22).

At a later period some of the Kenites separated from their brethren in the south, and went to northern Palestine (Judges iv. 11), where they existed in the time of Saul. The kindness which they had shown to Israel in the wilderness was gratefully remembered. "Ye showed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt," said Saul to them (I Sam. xv. 6); and so not only were they spared by him, but David allowed them to share in the spoil that he took from the Amalekites (ib. xxx. 29).

—Critical View:
According to the critical interpretation of the Biblical data, the Kenites were a clan settled on the southern border of Judah, originally more advanced in arts than the Hebrews, and from whom the latter learned much. In the time of David the Kenites were finally incorporated into the tribe of Judah (I Sam. xxx. 29; comp. ib. xxvii. 10). Their eponymous ancestor was Cain (Kain), to whose descendants J in Gen. iv. attributes the invention of the art of working bronze and iron, the use of instruments of music, etc. Sayce has inferred (in Hastings, "Dict. Bible," s.v.) that the Kenites were a tribe of smiths—a view to which J's statements would lend support.

Jethro, priest of Midian, and father-in-law of Moses, is said (Judges i. 16) to have been a Kenite.This indicates that the Kenites originally formed part of the Midianite tribe or tribes. In Ex. xviii. 12 et seq., according to E, Jethro initiates Moses and Aaron into the worship of Yhwh. Several modern scholars believe, in consequence of this statement, that Yhwh was a Kenite deity, and that from the Kenites through the agency of Moses his worship passed to the Israelites. This view, first proposed by Ghillany, afterward independently by Tiele, and more fully by Stade, has been more completely worked out by Budde; and is accepted by Guthe, Wildeboer, H. P. Smith, and Barton.

The Kenites, then, were a nomadic tribe, more advanced in the arts of life than Israel. Their habitat, according to the first Biblical reference to them, was in the Sinaitic peninsula (unless Horeb is to be sought in Edom), and a part of them, viz., Jethro and his family (Num. x. 29-32; Judges l.c.), migrated with the Israelites to the neighborhood of Jericho, afterward settled in the south of Judah, and were finally absorbed by that tribe.

Regimini militantis Ecclesiae (Latin for 'To the Government of the Church Militant') was the papal bull promulgated by Pope Paul III on September 27, 1540, which gave a first approval to the Society of Jesus, also known as the Jesuits, but limited the number of its members to sixty.

History
Ignatius of Loyola and his companions had made their way to Rome in October 1538, to offer their priestly services to the pope. As they were about to be dispersed by the various missions given them by the pope, the question arose as to whether they wished to remain spiritually "one". After prayer and discussion they decided positively: since Christ had brought them together, they felt it was His will they remain united. A charter was proposed to the pope, which was received favourably and ultimately given solemn approval in this Regimini Militantis Ecclesiae of 1540.[1][2] The first group of Jesuits, then known simply as "reformed priests", proceeded to unanimously elect Ignatius as their Superior General, despite his opposition.[3]

The final approval, with the removal of the restriction on the membership number, because they were not régimic[clarification needed], came in the bull Exposcit debitum (en: The duty requires ...) of July 21, 1550, issued by Pope Julius III.[2]

The papal text of 1540 included what is known as the Formula Instituti.[2] More developed Constitutions were gradually written by Ignatius and approved by the first General Chapter (called "General Congregation") of the Society of Jesus convened in 1558, two years after Ignatius' death. This first General Congregation also elected his successor.[3]

Clifford Lee Burton (February 10, 1962 – September 27, 1986) was an American musician who served as the bassist for the thrash metal band Metallica from 1982 until his death in 1986. He is renowned for his musicianship and influence.

Burton's early musical ventures include performing in bands such as EZ-Street and Agents of Misfortune, and frequently collaborating with guitarist Jim Martin. While performing in Los Angeles with Trauma, he was discovered by James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich who asked him to replace bassist Ron McGovney in Metallica. After the release of the band's first two albums, Kill 'Em All (1983) and Ride the Lightning (1984), Burton and Metallica achieved a worldwide breakthrough with Master of Puppets (1986), often cited as both the band's best work and one of the best metal albums of all time.

While touring in 1986 to support Master of Puppets, Burton was killed when the band's tour bus was involved in an accident. He received a posthumous writing credit on ...And Justice for All (1988) for the song "To Live Is to Die" and was posthumously inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Metallica in 2009. He also appeared in a 2011 Rolling Stone readers' poll recognizing the greatest bassists of all time,[1] and in Rolling Stone's list of the 50 greatest bass players of all time.[2]

Death
Burton's final performance with Metallica on September 26, 1986 was hosted at Solnahallen in Stockholm, Sweden on the Damage Inc. tour in support of the Master of Puppets album.[23] Their next scheduled show at the Saga Theater in Copenhagen, Denmark[24] had their tour bus driving south overnight along European route E4 (now G 557). Band members complained that the bunks on their tour bus were unsatisfactory and uncomfortable. The story of how Burton won the bunk differs between the two band members; as Kirk Hammett stated on VH1's Behind the Music, he and Burton drew cards, and Burton picked the ace of spades, thereby getting the first choice of bunk. Burton told Hammett "I want your bunk". Hammett replied "Fine, take my bunk, I'll sleep up front, it's probably better anyway".[25] However, Ulrich's version of the event was that Hammett and Burton drew straws, while Burton drew the long straw, winning the choice of bunk.[26] Burton was sleeping when, according to the driver, shortly before 7 a.m. on September 27, the bus skidded off the road 12 miles [19 km] north of Ljungby, just north of Dörarp,[27] and flipped onto the grass in Kronoberg County.[28] With no safety restraints on the bunks, Burton was thrown violently through one of the windows of the bus, which fell on top of him right afterwards, killing him instantly. He was 24 years old.

The bus driver later claimed that the crash was caused by the bus hitting a patch of black ice on the road, but Hetfield later stated that he first believed the bus flipped because the driver was intoxicated. Hetfield also claimed that he walked a lengthy distance along the road unsuccessfully searching for the point in which the bus lost traction from the black ice. When local freelance photographer Lennart Wennberg (who attended the crash-scene the following morning) was asked in a later interview about the likelihood that black ice caused the accident, he said it was "out of the question" because the road was dry and the temperature around 36 °F (2 °C), too warm for ice. This was confirmed by police who, like Hetfield, also found no ice on the road. Ljungby detective Arne Pettersson was reported in a local newspaper to have said the tracks at the accident site were exactly like ones seen when drivers fall asleep at the wheel. However, the driver stated under oath that he had slept during the day and was fully rested; his testimony was confirmed by the driver of a second tour bus that was carrying the band's crew and equipment.[27] The driver was determined not at fault for the accident and no charges were brought against him.[29]

Burton's body was cremated and the ashes were scattered at the Maxwell Ranch.[30] At the ceremony, the song "Orion" was played. Metallica would go on to hire Jason Newsted from Flotsam and Jetsam to replace Burton on October 28, 1986.[31][32] Both Ray and Jan Burton appeared at Newsted's second audition, in which Jan Burton embraced him following his hiring, telling Newsted "You are the one, Please be safe". He would remain with the band until his departure on January 17, 2001.[32][33]

Forfeiture Is Not Innocence: What Tinubu's 1993 Chicago Settlement Actually Means in Law

Letters from Stockholm — The Kio Solution By Kio Amachree
Every time the Chicago file resurfaces, the same defence is wheeled out from Abuja: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was never charged, never tried, never convicted. On 3 September 2026 the Presidency said it again, insisting that the Washington FOIA case is "a civil records-disclosure dispute" carrying no implications of criminal liability. Lawyers sympathetic to the President, among them Aloy Ejimakor, have made the same point in more careful language: the 1993 action was against property, not a person, and a civil forfeiture is not a finding of guilt.

As a statement of black-letter law, that is correct. As a defence of the man, it is hollow. This letter explains, as plainly as I can, what a civil forfeiture is, what it required in 1993, what Tinubu chose to do when he was confronted with one, and why the absence of a conviction is not the absence of a stain.

What happened in Chicago

In July 1993 the United States Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois filed Case No. 93 C 4483 before Judge John A. Nordberg. It was an in rem action, meaning the defendant was not Bola Tinubu but the money itself: funds in accounts at First Heritage Bank and Citibank, more than $1.4 million in all, which the government said were traceable to a Chicago heroin-distribution network operating between roughly 1988 and 1991. The complaint rested on the sworn affidavit of IRS Special Agent Kevin Moss, who laid out the movement of money through those accounts and their connection to persons already arrested in the heroin investigation.

Tinubu, through counsel, contested the action and asserted that the money was legitimately his. Then, rather than take that claim to trial, he settled. On 4 October 1993 the court entered an order under which $460,000 was forfeited to the United States and the remaining funds were released to him. The case was closed with prejudice. He walked away with most of the money, and the United States government kept $460,000 as the proceeds of narcotics trafficking.

What the law required of him in 1993

Here is the part the Presidency never explains. Under the federal civil forfeiture regime in force in 1993, before the Civil Asset Forfeiture Reform Act of 2000, the government's burden was strikingly light. It needed only to show probable cause to believe the property was connected to drug trafficking. Once it did so, the burden shifted to the claimant. If Bola Tinubu wanted his money back, the law required him to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the funds came from a legitimate source and had nothing to do with heroin.

Think about what that means. A man who says his money is clean, who has bank records, business documents and a legitimate explanation, has every incentive to go to court and prove it. The standard is not "beyond reasonable doubt." It is the ordinary civil standard: more likely than not. A claimant with a lawful source of $460,000 in 1993, an enormous sum, would have a paper trail. Tinubu did not produce one to a judge. He signed the money over.

Why a settlement is, in substance, an acknowledgment

Lawyers for the President will say that a forfeiture settlement contains no admission of guilt, and that is true of the paperwork. Settlements are routinely drafted without admissions. But the law recognises a difference between what a document admits and what a person's conduct acknowledges.

A forfeiture is not a fine. A fine punishes you and lets you keep what is yours. A forfeiture takes property on the specific legal theory that it never lawfully belonged to you, because it is the fruit or instrumentality of a crime. When Tinubu agreed to forfeit $460,000, he agreed to a court order transferring that money to the United States on the ground that it was traceable to heroin sales. He did not agree to pay a penalty; he agreed that the government could keep drug money. The order stands on the public record to this day with his name on it. That is what I mean when I say the settlement is an acknowledgment. He was offered the chance to prove the money was clean. He declined and gave it up.

A person who forfeits proceeds is, in the plain meaning of the word, someone who has been made to disgorge the benefit of a crime. That he negotiated the amount down from $1.4 million to $460,000 does not change the character of what was surrendered. It only tells us that the government and his lawyers agreed on how much of the pile was demonstrably tainted.

Why there was no criminal case

The Presidency treats the absence of an indictment as vindication. It is nothing of the sort. There is a simpler explanation, and it lies in geography.

Between 1988 and 1993, when the Chicago investigation was live, Bola Tinubu was not living in the United States. He was in Nigeria, where by 1992 he had been elected a senator. Federal prosecutors bringing narcotics conspiracy charges against a foreign national residing abroad face extradition, diplomacy and delay; bringing a forfeiture action against money already sitting in Chicago bank accounts faces none of those obstacles. The property was within the court's reach. The man was not. Prosecutors did what prosecutors do: they took the case they could win in a courtroom without a defendant in the dock.

Had Tinubu been resident in Chicago in 1993, with his name in an IRS agent's sworn affidavit tying his accounts to a heroin ring whose members were already under arrest, it is my firm opinion that he would have been arrested, arraigned and required to answer the same allegations in a criminal court, where the burden would have fallen on the government but where the evidence in that affidavit would have been laid before a jury. That is not a legal finding. It is the reasonable inference any honest observer draws from the fact that the other men named in that investigation were not offered a settlement; they were prosecuted.

What thirty-three years of silence tells us

If the 1993 record were the whole story, it might be argued that a young man settled an inconvenient case and moved on. But the story has not ended, because Tinubu has not let it end.

Since 2022, when the transparency litigant Aaron Greenspan asked the FBI and DEA for their records on the investigation, the President of Nigeria has intervened personally in an American court, in Greenspan v. Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys, Civil Action No. 23-1816 before Judge Beryl Howell, to keep those records sealed. In April 2025 Judge Howell rejected the agencies' refusal even to confirm the records existed and ordered them searched and processed. The FBI has since released 399 heavily redacted pages, and on 20 August 2026, in a motion signed by US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, it told the court that the full basis for its remaining redactions could not even be stated in public and would have to be delivered to the judge under seal. On 28 August the President filed his own opposition, invoking FOIA Exemption 7(C) on the ground that release would be an unwarranted invasion of his personal privacy. Replies are due on 11 September and 18 September.

Consider the logic of the President's own position. If, as Abuja insists, the 1993 matter was an innocent misunderstanding about a civil case that established nothing, then the files can only help him. An innocent man wants the record out. Instead the sitting head of a sovereign state is spending public credibility and private legal fees to keep an American judge from letting Nigerians read what American investigators wrote about him. In law, a party's effort to suppress evidence permits an adverse inference. In politics, it permits a blunter one: there is something in those files he does not want his people to see.

The distinction that matters

So let us be precise, because precision is what the Presidency claims to want. Bola Tinubu has not been convicted of a drug offence, and I do not say he has. What I say is this. A United States court, on the sworn evidence of a federal agent, found probable cause that money in his accounts was heroin proceeds. The law gave him the opportunity to prove otherwise on the lowest standard the civil courts know, and he chose not to take it. He surrendered $460,000 to the United States government under an order describing it as the proceeds of narcotics trafficking. He was beyond the reach of a criminal court at the time, and the record suggests that others within its reach were prosecuted. And for the last three years, as President, he has fought in open court to prevent the underlying files from seeing daylight.

Nigerians may draw their own conclusions from that record. Mine is that a man who forfeits drug money to a foreign government, and then as head of state fights to bury the evidence of why, is not fit to hold the office he occupies. The Presidency is right that this is not a criminal trial. It is something a head of state should fear more: a public one.

Nigeria belongs to Nigerians.

All references to criminal conduct are allegations drawn from public court records and sworn filings. The 1993 proceeding was a civil in rem forfeiture; President Tinubu has never been charged with or convicted of a criminal offence in connection with it and has consistently denied wrongdoing. The opinions expressed are the author's own.

PARK AND FLEECE: MAN POSES AS LOT ATTENDANT, CHARGES SHOPPERS $8 A SPOT FOR A WEEK

SPRINGFIELD, ILLINOIS — Ray Duchesne, 38, was charged Friday after allegedly posing as a lot attendant outside a busy shopping center for an entire week, charging unsuspecting shoppers $8 per parking spot with a homemade "PARKING $8 PER SPOT PER WEEK" sign and a laminated badge that read "LOT ATTENDANT."

Investigators say he never once worked for the property or the store.

Detectives say Duchesne wore a reflective vest purchased from a hardware store the same morning he started
Witnesses report he greeted every car personally and handed out handwritten receipts torn from a notepad
Shoppers say he offered a "loyalty discount" for anyone paying for the full week upfront in cash
Investigators say he collected roughly $340 total before a store manager finally asked to see his employee badge
He allegedly told confronted shoppers the lot was "technically unregulated, so somebody had to step up"
Detectives say he had reportedly run the same scheme at two other shopping centers earlier in the year

Regular shoppers reportedly admitted they simply assumed the lot had always charged for parking and never questioned it.

"In twenty-one years with this department, I've investigated a lot of scams, but never one that ran on foot traffic and a clipboard," said Detective Sergeant Wayne Ostrander, a 21-year veteran of the Springfield Police Department.

The vest and badge were seized as evidence. The $340 has not been recovered.

He didn't own the lot. He just owned the moment.
Rain makes people believe almost anything.

text:
Today in History 
September 5th
1940
Born on this Day
Raquel Welch was an American actress and international sex symbol who became one of Hollywood’s most recognizable stars of the 1960s and 1970s. She was born Jo Raquel Tejada on September 5, 1940, in Chicago, Illinois, and died on February 15, 2023, in Los Angeles, California, at the age of 82.

Welch was the daughter of Armando Carlos Tejada Urquizo, a Bolivian-born aeronautical engineer, and Josephine Sarah Hall, an American of English ancestry. Her family moved to San Diego when she was young, and she began studying ballet as a child. As a teenager, she entered beauty contests and won several titles. She later attended San Diego State College on a theater scholarship and worked in local television before pursuing acting professionally.

Her breakthrough came in 1966. She appeared in the science-fiction film Fantastic Voyage, but it was her role as Loana in One Million Years B.C. that transformed her into an international celebrity. Although she had relatively little dialogue in the film, promotional images of Welch wearing a fur bikini became some of the most famous movie publicity photographs of the era.

Welch subsequently worked to establish herself as more than a glamour figure. Her films included Bedazzled (1967), Bandolero! (1968), 100 Rifles (1969), Myra Breckinridge (1970), Hannie Caulder (1971), The Three Musketeers (1973), and The Four Musketeers (1974). She won a Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy for The Three Musketeers.

Her career was also significant culturally. At a time when Hollywood offered relatively few prominent roles to performers of Latin American heritage, Welch became one of the industry’s biggest stars. Interestingly, the public generally knew her by the surname Welch, which came from her first husband, James Welch, rather than by her birth surname Tejada.

Welch married four times: to James Welch, Patrick Curtis, André Weinfeld, and Richard Palmer. She had two children with James Welch, Damon Welch and actress Tahnee Welch.

Beyond movies, Welch appeared extensively on television and stage and developed successful business ventures connected with beauty, fitness, and wigs. She published the fitness and lifestyle book Raquel: The Raquel Welch Total Beauty and Fitness Program in 1984 and later wrote the memoir Raquel: Beyond the Cleavage in 2010.

By the end of her career, Welch had become an enduring figure in American popular culture. While the famous One Million Years B.C. image initially defined her public persona, her career ultimately lasted more than five decades and encompassed film, television, theater, fitness, writing, and business. #OTD

text:
THE WAR THAT IS NOT A WAR
A Guru Nanga tale, part 6 of 12

Previously: $2.98 to $4.56, a record Labor Day, “if they rise, they rise.” The one thing was offered in writing and the answer was a blockade. A strait was declared a territory, then a Trump Strait, then “just thrown out there.”

III. THE QUESTION OF WHO IS PAYING (CONTINUED)

LEO: And the people at the pump?

NANGA: An Uber driver in Oakland, John Mejia. Guru Nanga knows the gas stations he means. He said: “A few weeks ago, I filled up my hybrid car for $36. Now it’s $60, so I don’t drive as much.” A trucker in Houston named Eddie Esquivel, whose weekly diesel doubled: “You got truck payments, you got to buy tires, you got to do oil changes, and you got a family,” and then: “This is killing us.” Consumer sentiment in May was the lowest number the University of Michigan has recorded since it began asking. The Secretary of War, asked at a hearing what gas had cost before the war, said: “Well, it depends on where you live. If you live in California, it’s 8 bucks.”

LEO: You live in California.

NANGA: I do. I filled the Camry on February 27 for four dollars and sixty-four cents. I have the receipt. The Secretary has not asked for it. Fewer than five of ten thousand five hundred stations in the state were at eight dollars. Guru Nanga has driven past two of them. They are near the airport and they know what they are.

LEO: And the reserve? I read there was a reserve.

NANGA: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is sixty salt caverns on the Gulf coast. It fell to 289.7 million barrels last week, the lowest since 1982, and is heading below the floor the law sets for routine withdrawals. Congress appropriated $171 million to refill something estimated to need $20 billion. In 1982 Guru Nanga was thirteen and also running low. He recovered. He is less sure about the caverns.

LEO: The dead.

NANGA: Eighteen, on the day before the website changed. Six at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait on the second day. Six in a tanker aircraft over Iraq on March 12. Three in a barracks in Jordan in July. Sergeant Declan Coady of West Des Moines was twenty. Private Isabella Gonzales of Carrollton, Texas, was nineteen. The President went to Dover and said: “For me it’s one of the hardest things to do as a president. But it has to be done.” The next day he said: “one is too many, but it’s 18. Whereas in Vietnam, we lost 200,000.” Guru Nanga has a rule about the dead. He does not joke near them. He will only say that the comparison to Vietnam is the first time this administration has volunteered the word war for what the men died in, and it did so to make the number look small.

The Pope did not say anything. Guru Nanga found this to be the correct response and wrote it down as such.

Next: the children, and a stop.

text:
THE WAR THAT IS NOT A WAR
A Guru Nanga tale, part 5 of 12

Previously: one capital says it is not a war and the other says it is existential. A cell changed its own history in two days. Both governments cite Venezuela, one as a menu and one as a warning. One cancels the clock. One cancels the prisoner.

III. THE QUESTION OF WHO IS PAYING

LEO: You are an American. What has it cost your neighbours?

NANGA: I will start with the smallest number, because it is the largest. Regular gasoline was $2.98 a gallon on the morning of February 28. It crossed $4 on March 31, the biggest one-month rise on record. It peaked at $4.56 in May, with all fifty states above $4. Labor Day was the most expensive in American history, and diesel, which prices everything on a shelf, set an all-time record of $5.85 yesterday. The President was asked about this on March 5 and said: “if they rise, they rise.” They rose.

LEO: He is known for a different position on prices.

NANGA: He is. A woman named Kelly Gravlin filled a Toyota 4Runner at a Costco in Michigan for $70.73 and said, of the President: “From a president who ran on getting gas prices low.” On May 12 the President was asked whether Americans’ finances were influencing his search for a deal. He said: “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody. I focus on one thing: We cannot allow Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon. That’s it.”

LEO: That is at least a clear objective.

NANGA: It is. Iran’s president said last month that Iran was “prepared to put it in writing that we do not intend to build a nuclear weapon.” So the one thing has been offered in writing, and the answer was a blockade. Guru Nanga has negotiated with contractors. When the other side offers you the one thing, you take the one thing. You do not declare the strait a territory.

LEO: Was it declared?

NANGA: On August 14: “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.” On September 2 he posted “TRUMP STRAIT???” and, asked about it that evening, said: “No, no … it was just thrown out there.”

Next: the people at the pump, sixty salt caverns, and the dead.
