text:
Trade, Tariffs, and Interest Rates: What Trump Is Actually Talking About — Explained for People Who Hate Finance

At first, Donald Trump’s argument sounds extremely simple.

The United States buys a lot from another country.

That country sells more to America than America sells back.

Therefore, America has a trade deficit.

Trump’s conclusion is essentially:

“They need access to the American market more than we need access to theirs. So why aren’t we using that power?”

That is the core idea behind almost everything he says in the video.

But to understand whether the argument makes sense, you need to separate several things that are constantly mixed together in political discussions:

trade deficits, tariffs, economic leverage, government debt, and interest rates.

They are related.

They are not the same thing.

And once you understand the difference, the entire argument becomes much easier to follow.

First: What Is a Trade Deficit?

Forget economics textbooks for a moment.

Imagine that you live in the United States.

During one year, Americans buy $120 billion worth of products from Country X.

Country X buys only $50 billion worth of American products.

The calculation is:

$120 billion imported − $50 billion exported = $70 billion trade deficit

The United States therefore has a $70 billion trade deficit with Country X.

That sounds terrible when politicians say it.

But here is the first extremely important point:

A trade deficit is not the same thing as losing $70 billion.

Americans did not put $70 billion into a hole and burn it.

They received products in exchange.

Maybe they received cars.

Maybe computers.

Maybe medicine.

Maybe oil.

Maybe steel.

Maybe machinery.

Maybe food.

If you spend $1,500 buying a laptop, you have a "$1,500 trade deficit" with the computer store.

The computer store bought nothing from you.

But you did not necessarily lose $1,500.

You exchanged $1,500 for a computer that you wanted.

International trade is obviously much more complicated, but this basic distinction matters enormously.

A trade deficit measures an imbalance in flows of goods and services.

It is not automatically a measure of how much money a country has "lost."

So Why Does Trump Care So Much About Trade Deficits?

Because Trump looks at international trade differently from many traditional economists.

Traditional economists often emphasize:

What can consumers buy cheaply?

Trump emphasizes:

Who controls the industrial capacity, factories, supply chains, and bargaining power?

Those are very different perspectives.

Suppose America buys most of an important product from another country.

Cheap imports may be wonderful for American consumers.

But then imagine that the product is strategically important.

Semiconductors.

Medicine.

Military components.

Energy.

Steel.

Critical minerals.

Now dependence starts becoming a national-security question.

Imagine that a country says:

"We will no longer ship this product to you."

Suddenly the cheap price you enjoyed for twenty years does not seem quite as important.

This is where Trump's trade philosophy becomes easier to understand.

He is not merely asking:

"Are imports cheap?"

He is asking:

"Who needs whom more?"

The Switzerland Example

In the video, Trump essentially says that if America stopped trading with Switzerland, America could no longer have a trade deficit with Switzerland.

Mathematically, that is true in the narrowest possible sense.

If trade becomes zero:

Exports = $0.

Imports = $0.

Trade balance = $0.

Congratulations.

You eliminated the trade deficit.

But you also eliminated the trade.

That distinction is enormous.

Imagine you spend $5,000 per year at a supermarket.

The supermarket spends $0 at your house.

You therefore have a massive "trade deficit" with your supermarket.

You can eliminate that deficit tomorrow.

Simply stop buying food.

Your deficit disappears.

Your problem is that your food disappears too.

This is why economists usually do not treat eliminating a bilateral trade deficit as automatically equivalent to becoming richer.

The real question is:

What were we getting from that trade, what would replace it, and at what cost?

Switzerland, for example, is known for industries including pharmaceuticals, chemicals, specialized machinery, watches, and financial services.

If America suddenly stopped importing products it currently purchases from Switzerland, Americans would need substitutes.

Perhaps American companies could produce them.

Perhaps companies in Germany, Japan, France, South Korea, or elsewhere could replace them.

Perhaps prices would rise.

Perhaps American production would expand.

Those second-order effects determine whether the policy makes economic sense.

The number "trade deficit = bad" does not tell you enough.

Then We Get to Tariffs

Trump's preferred weapon is often the tariff.

A tariff is basically a tax on imported goods.

Suppose a Canadian company sells something to an American importer for:

$100

Now imagine the United States imposes a 25% tariff.

The importer may have to pay:

$25 in tariff

So the landed cost becomes approximately:

$125

Who actually absorbs that $25?

That is where the real economic battle begins.

The Canadian company might lower its selling price.

The American importer might accept lower profits.

The American retailer might accept lower profits.

The customer might pay a higher price.

Usually the cost can be distributed among several parties.

That is why saying:

"Foreign countries pay the tariff"

is too simplistic.

The tariff is collected by the U.S. government, but the economic burden can be shared across producers, importers, retailers, and consumers.

But Trump Is Thinking One Step Beyond Tariffs

His stronger argument is essentially:

"What if we simply refuse to trade with you?"

That is much more powerful than a normal tariff.

Suppose Country A sells America $200 billion of products every year.

America sells Country A only $40 billion.

America has an enormous consumer market.

Country A's companies may depend heavily on American customers.

Then America can theoretically say:

"Accept our conditions, or lose access to our market."

Now we are no longer talking only about economics.

We are talking about geoeconomic power.

The U.S. market itself becomes a weapon.

That part of Trump's argument is not difficult to understand.

America is one of the world's largest consumer markets.

Access to American customers is enormously valuable.

If a foreign industry depends heavily on that access, Washington possesses leverage.

The harder question is whether using that leverage produces more benefits than collateral damage.

Canada Makes This Much Easier to Understand

Trump claims in the video that ending all trade with Canada would save the United States $90 billion.

That statement needs to be understood very carefully.

Suppose, purely as an example, America imports:

$400 billion

from Canada and exports:

$310 billion

to Canada.

The difference would be:

$90 billion

Someone might look at the number and say:

"We are losing $90 billion to Canada."

But that is not economically equivalent to losing $90 billion.

America received $400 billion worth of goods and services.

Canada received $310 billion worth of American goods and services.

Stopping all trade does not magically deposit $90 billion into the U.S. Treasury.

It means both sides stop receiving those goods and services.

And Canada is deeply integrated with American supply chains.

Think about something as ordinary as a car.

A component might cross the U.S.-Canada border several times before the finished automobile reaches a dealership.

An engine component could be manufactured in Michigan.

Sent to Ontario.

Installed into a larger assembly.

Sent back to Ohio.

Combined with another component.

Then sent somewhere else.

Modern production networks often do not respect the simple mental picture:

"America makes American things and Canada makes Canadian things."

Factories form networks.

Closing the border economically could disrupt the entire network.

Consider Canadian Oil

This provides an even clearer example.

America imports significant quantities of Canadian energy.

Imagine the United States stopped buying Canadian crude oil tomorrow.

You could proudly say:

"Our imports from Canada fell!"

Excellent.

But American refineries still need crude oil.

So what happens next?

They might have to buy oil from somewhere else.

Transportation costs could change.

The type of crude available could be different.

Refineries configured for particular grades of oil might face complications.

Prices could move.

Supply chains would have to reorganize.

So the important question is not simply:

"Did imports fall?"

The important question is:

"What replaced them?"

This is one of the most important questions in economics.

Whenever someone says:

"We will eliminate X!"

ask:

"And what replaces X?"

That question destroys a remarkable amount of bad economic reasoning.

Now We Arrive at the Much Bigger Issue: Interest Rates

This is arguably the more important part of Trump's argument.

Trump says that some countries pay around:

0.5%

while the United States pays around:

4%

and argues that this makes no sense because America supposedly has superior creditworthiness and economic power.

His desired rate is around:

1% or even 0.5%.

Why does this matter so much?

Because the U.S. government owes an enormous amount of money.

When you owe a small amount of money, interest rates are annoying.

When you owe tens of trillions of dollars, interest rates become one of the central questions of government finance.

Think About a Mortgage

Suppose you owe:

$500,000

At a 1% interest rate, simplified annual interest is:

$5,000

At 4%:

$20,000

Same house.

Same debt.

Completely different financing cost.

Now multiply that concept to the scale of a national government.

The difference between borrowing at 1% and 4% becomes enormous.

That is the world Trump is looking at.

Why Does He Mention "$650 Billion Per Percentage Point"?

Trump says that every additional 1 percentage point of interest costs the United States $650 billion.

The basic concept he is pointing toward is legitimate:

Higher borrowing costs can eventually produce enormous additional government interest expenses.

But you should not interpret the number as:

"The Federal Reserve raises rates 1%, and tomorrow the government instantly owes another $650 billion."

Government debt does not work that cleanly.

Treasury securities have different maturities.

Some mature in weeks.

Some in months.

Some in years.

Some in decades.

Imagine America issued a 10-year Treasury bond years ago at 2%.

If market interest rates rise to 5% tomorrow, the government does not suddenly start paying 5% on that existing fixed-rate bond.

Its contractual coupon remains what it was.

But eventually the bond matures.

If the government still needs the money, it refinances.

Now the new debt may be issued at a much higher rate.

That is where the pain gradually enters the budget.

Imagine Refinancing a Giant Mortgage Every Year

Suppose your family owes:

$1 million

But the debt is divided into pieces.

$100,000 needs refinancing this year.

Another $100,000 next year.

Another portion later.

When interest rates rise, your entire debt expense does not explode immediately.

The expensive refinancing spreads through your debt over time.

That is roughly the concept you should keep in your head when thinking about government borrowing costs.

This is why sustained high interest rates can become much more dangerous than a brief spike.

The longer rates remain elevated, the more old cheap debt gets replaced with newer expensive debt.

Why Can't America Simply Demand a 0.5% Interest Rate?

This is where the argument becomes much more complicated.

Interest rates are not a reward handed to countries because they are powerful.

Rates reflect many forces.

Inflation.

Expected inflation.

Central-bank policy.

Economic growth.

Demand for bonds.

Currency risk.

Fiscal deficits.

Debt issuance.

Investor expectations.

Global capital flows.

Imagine two borrowers.

Borrower A is extremely wealthy but inflation is running at 5%.

Borrower B lives in an economy with virtually no inflation.

It is entirely possible for Borrower B's country to have lower nominal interest rates.

Why?

Because investors care about what their money will actually be worth later.

Inflation Is the Part Beginners Often Miss

Imagine I offer you a bond.

It pays:

1% per year.

Sounds fine.

But inflation is:

5% per year.

You earn 1%.

Prices rise 5%.

Your purchasing power is deteriorating.

That is not very attractive.

Now imagine another country offers a bond paying only:

0.5%

but its inflation rate is approximately zero.

Suddenly that 0.5% does not look ridiculous.

This is why comparing countries by saying:

"They pay 0.5%, so America should pay 0.5%"

can be misleading.

You need to compare the entire monetary and inflation environment.

There Is Also a Huge Difference Between "The Interest Rate" and "An Interest Rate"

People often speak about "the interest rate" as if one giant interest rate controls everything.

It does not.

There are many rates.

Central-bank policy rates.

Three-month Treasury yields.

Two-year Treasury yields.

Ten-year Treasury yields.

Thirty-year Treasury yields.

Mortgage rates.

Corporate bond yields.

Credit-card rates.

Bank deposit rates.

They influence each other, but they are not identical.

So when someone says:

"America pays 4%"

the first financially literate response should be:

"Which rate?"

That question matters.

The Federal Reserve Also Complicates the Story

The president cannot simply declare:

"Interest rates are now 0.5%."

The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy through its own institutional process.

And even the Federal Reserve does not perfectly dictate long-term Treasury yields.

Investors in the bond market matter too.

Suppose the government desperately wants ten-year borrowing costs of 1%.

But investors believe inflation will average 4%.

Why would investors enthusiastically lend money for ten years at 1%?

They may demand a higher yield.

The government can influence financial conditions enormously.

But markets still price risk, inflation, growth, and supply and demand.

Here Is the Paradox

Trump's basic concern about government interest costs is important.

Imagine a government running large deficits while interest rates remain high.

The government must borrow more.

Higher debt means more interest payments.

More interest payments worsen the budget deficit.

Larger deficits require more borrowing.

More borrowing creates more debt.

And more debt creates more interest expense.

You can get a feedback loop:

Deficit → borrowing → debt → interest expense → bigger deficit → more borrowing

That is the genuinely important financial issue hidden underneath the political rhetoric.

And it deserves far more attention than many people give it.

Why Very Low Rates Are Not Free Money

Now imagine the Federal Reserve somehow pushes rates from 4% to 0.5%.

Fantastic for government borrowing costs.

Fantastic for many borrowers.

Mortgage rates could eventually fall.

Businesses could finance investments more cheaply.

Asset prices might rise.

But there is another side.

Cheap money can stimulate demand.

More borrowing.

More spending.

More speculation.

More asset purchases.

If the economy cannot increase production sufficiently, prices may rise.

That means inflation.

And if inflation accelerates, the central bank may eventually be forced to raise rates again.

So politicians often love low interest rates.

Central banks have to worry about the consequences.

Here Is a Simple Example

Imagine an island with:

100 houses

and buyers collectively have:

$10 million available to spend.

Now credit becomes extremely cheap.

Suddenly buyers can access:

$20 million

But there are still only:

100 houses.

Did the island magically become twice as rich?

No.

Much of the new purchasing power may simply bid up house prices.

Cheap credit can stimulate real investment.

But it can also inflate asset prices.

That is why "lower interest rates" and "more prosperity" are not automatically identical.

Now Connect Trade Policy and Interest Rates

This is where the discussion becomes genuinely interesting.

Trump wants two things simultaneously:

stronger trade protection
and
much lower interest rates.

But those policies can sometimes pull in opposite directions.

Suppose tariffs make imported goods more expensive.

A $1,000 imported appliance now costs $1,150.

A $30,000 vehicle becomes more expensive because imported components cost more.

Construction materials become more expensive.

Businesses pass some of those costs to customers.

That can contribute to inflationary pressure.

If inflation rises, the Federal Reserve may become less willing to cut interest rates aggressively.

So you can encounter a tension:

Tariffs may support domestic production and strategic independence, but they can also increase prices.

Meanwhile:

Lower rates make borrowing cheaper, but they can also stimulate demand and inflation.

Economic policymaking is full of these trade-offs.

There is rarely a magical button labeled:

MAKE AMERICA RICHER.

Then Why Use Tariffs at All?

Because tariffs can have strategic purposes beyond immediately lowering consumer prices.

Suppose producing a critical component in America costs:

$120
while importing it costs:
$100.

Without protection, companies naturally import it.

American factories close.

Workers leave the industry.

Technical knowledge disappears.

Supply chains relocate.

Twenty years later, America depends almost completely on foreign production.

Then a geopolitical crisis occurs.

Suddenly that missing domestic capacity becomes extremely valuable.

A tariff might intentionally make the $100 imported product cost $125, allowing the $120 American producer to compete.

Consumers pay somewhat more.

But domestic industrial capacity survives.

Whether that trade-off is worthwhile depends on the industry.

For toys?

Maybe not.

For advanced semiconductors?

Potentially much more important.

For defense equipment?

Very different calculation.

For essential medicine?

Again, different.

This is why serious trade policy needs to be discussed sector by sector.

Trump's Strongest Argument Is Not Really About Accounting

It is about leverage.

Suppose another country depends on America for 70% of its exports.

America depends on that country for only 5% of its imports.

Who has more bargaining power?

Probably America.

Trump looks at those asymmetries and asks:

Why aren't we extracting better terms?

That is essentially a business negotiation mindset applied to international relations.

Access to American consumers becomes a negotiating asset.

Tariffs become pressure.

Import restrictions become pressure.

Export controls become pressure.

Market access becomes pressure.

That part is easier to understand if you stop thinking about Trump as giving an economics lecture.

He is describing a negotiation strategy.

But Negotiation Power Has a Cost

Imagine Walmart tells an important supplier:

"Cut your price 40%, or we never buy from you again."

Maybe the supplier panics and agrees.

Walmart wins.

But suppose the supplier produces something Walmart cannot easily replace.

Then Walmart has just created a problem for itself.

Countries face the same constraint.

Leverage is only powerful when the threat is credible.

If America says:

"We do not need your products."

but American factories desperately need those products tomorrow morning, the foreign country knows America's threat has limits.

This is why supply-chain mapping matters.

Before threatening to eliminate trade, policymakers need to know:

What exactly are we importing?

Who uses it?

Can we replace it?

How quickly?

At what price?

What happens if the other country retaliates?

Those questions are much more important than the headline trade-deficit number.

There Is Another Thing Most People Miss: Foreigners Can Send the Dollars Back

Suppose America imports more goods than it exports.

Where do the dollars go?

They do not disappear.

Foreign exporters receive dollars.

What can they do with those dollars?

They might buy American stocks.

They might buy American companies.

They might invest in American factories.

They might buy real estate.

They might buy U.S. Treasury securities.

In other words, a trade deficit is connected to international capital flows.

America can import more than it exports partly because foreigners are willing to hold American financial assets.

This is one reason the subject becomes much more complicated than:

"We sent them $100, they sent us $50, therefore we lost $50."

The international financial system is a loop.

Goods move one direction.

Capital can move another.

The Dollar Changes Everything

The United States has another unusual characteristic.

The dollar is one of the world's dominant reserve and transaction currencies.

Companies and governments around the world want dollar assets.

Banks need dollars.

International trade is often invoiced in dollars.

Central banks hold dollar reserves.

Investors buy U.S. Treasury securities.

That creates extraordinary financial advantages for the United States.

America is not simply another country participating in global trade.

It also supplies one of the central monetary assets of the global financial system.

That gives the United States enormous power.

But it also creates strange consequences.

Global demand for dollars and U.S. financial assets can help finance American deficits.

That can also contribute to persistent trade imbalances.

So if you seriously want to understand American trade deficits, you eventually have to understand the dollar system too.

Now Go Back to the Numbers in the Video

Trump mentions roughly:

0.5% interest rates in some other countries.

4% for the United States.

A desired rate of:

1% or 0.5%.

He claims approximately:

$650 billion

of cost for every percentage point of interest.

And approximately:

$90 billion

of savings from eliminating trade with Canada.

These numbers sound powerful because they are enormous.

But never let a large number end your thinking.

Let it start your thinking.

When someone says:

"$90 billion!"

ask:

$90 billion of what?

A trade deficit?

Government spending?

Tax revenue?

Economic output?

Imports?

Net savings?

Those are completely different concepts.

When someone says:

"4% interest!"

ask:

Which interest rate?

Policy rate?

Treasury yield?

Average government borrowing cost?

Ten-year bond?

Short-term debt?

Again, completely different concepts.

This Is the Financial Habit You Actually Need

You do not need a finance degree.

You need to learn to ask better questions.

Whenever politicians discuss trade:

What exactly is being imported?

What exactly is being exported?

Who benefits?

Who pays?

What replaces the imports?

Whenever politicians discuss tariffs:

Who legally pays the tariff?

Who economically absorbs the cost?

Can domestic production expand?

How long would that take?

Whenever politicians discuss interest rates:

Which rate?

Why is it at that level?

What is inflation doing?

How much debt is refinancing?

What happens if rates stay high?

That is already enough to put you ahead of an astonishing number of people arguing about economics online.

text:
This yellow Cardinal is a one-in-10-million genetic anomaly.

Arlene and John McDaniel were recently treated to an extraordinary sight at their backyard bird feeder in Michigan: a brilliant yellow northern cardinal.

While northern cardinals are famous for their vivid red plumage, this striking golden variant is incredibly rare. According to ornithologist Geoffrey Hill of Auburn University, the odds of encountering a yellow cardinal are roughly one in 10 million. With an estimated population of about 50 million northern cardinals across North America, experts believe only around five such birds exist at any given time — making this sighting a once-in-a-lifetime event.

The bird’s unusual color results from a rare “knockout mutation” that interrupts the normal pigmentation process. Normally, cardinals convert dietary pigments into red feathers through a two-step enzymatic reaction. In this case, the genetic mutation blocks that process, causing the feathers to remain a bright, vibrant yellow instead.

First scientifically documented in 1989, these rare yellow cardinals offer valuable insights into avian genetics and the intricate DNA mechanisms that shape the natural world. What began as a surprise visitor at a backyard feeder has become a beautiful reminder of nature’s occasional and stunning genetic surprises.

[Hill, G. Genetic Components and Rare Pigmentation in the Northern Cardinal. Auburn University Department of Biological Sciences]

𝘐𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘥𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘛. 𝘍. 𝘛𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦, ‘𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺’ 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘢 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘪𝘯𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘳𝘥𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘴𝘱𝘢𝘤𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦, 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘺𝘰𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵. 𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘪𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘤𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘥, 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘲𝘶𝘦 𝘨𝘪𝘧𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘩𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘯 𝘥𝘰𝘤𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥 𝘪𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭.[1]

I drew a line between late medieval theology, and Thomas’s impact, and the developments of Post Reformation Reformed orthodoxy. It is difficult to generalize the period because it is made up of various characters and personages with just as various perspectives and theological conclusions. But in general, the style of classical theism the reformed orthodox appropriated, and developed, came with the Aristotelian tendencies; even if they wanted to affirm rather than deny (so Aristotle) creatio ex nihilo (‘creation out of nothing’). That’s what this discussion we are engaging with is about: viz. creation out of nothing, and the attendant understanding of contingency that follows.

My contention is that the theologies produced by the Post Reformed orthodox theologians were not altogether successful in emphasizing the freedom and thus requisite contingency that would attend such Divine freedom in a God-world relation. The consequent, one of them, is that the way people understand God’s relationship to the world, in the Christian Aristotelian model, is one wherein we end up with a Decretal God who relates to creation through decrees and the attending doctrine of causality (predeterminism that ends up making God in Christ in the incarnation a predicate of creation rather than its predicator; thus rupturing God’s person in Christ from his work in Christ). This continues to be an issue that plagues the current excavation work that people like Mike Allen and Scott Swain, among other young stalwarts, are engaged in at this very moment. Because folks like this ostensibly spy problems in modern theology they paradigmatically reject the idea that a fruitful or corrective understanding of a doctrine of God might be found there. They’d rather cast their lot with the so called tradition, and appeal to the natural theology required to make such an appeal.

At the end of the day I’m left wondering: what makes an idea about God orthodox? Is it really the period of ideation and development that said ideas developed within; and by whom? Or is there a greater regulative principle we ought to consider? What if Holy Scripture was in fact the norma normans and principium theologiae that so many of these younger evangelical theologians laudably affirm (as good Reformed thinkers). What if Scripture’s res (reality) was in fact the risen Christ, and the viva vox Dei (living voice of God) was in fact greater than the tradition that so many of these theologians appeal to as regulative for their own recovery projects? Some fear a Socinianism, a fallacious biblicism run amok, when they hear such words as mine. But what if the reality of Holy Scripture still speaks fresh and new words today, such that the tradition itself is called into relief when standing in the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ? What if theology has an eschatological character to it, such that theology itself is always only a proximate endeavor that requires renovation over and again as it is pressed up and further into the lively reality it claims to be speaking of (rather than about) and to?

These are the kinds of questions and issues that continue to drive me as a Christian thinker. I don’t see a lot of fresh work being done in the theological realm, per se. Instead I see a constant desire to re-iterize what has already been said, a desire to return to the ‘old paths’ to the golden age of a theological yesteryear that somehow eclipses the present and its ability to produce constructive theologies on their own terms in dialogue with the living voice of God in Holy Scripture and its reality in Jesus Christ. This is not to suggest that the categories of the tradition do not offer valuable trajectories and insights, but it is to suggest that a repristination of these periods is of only relative value for the Christian churches catholic. The catholicizing reality that binds the church together is not tradition, but the risen Christ; as we proclaim his coming in eucharistic unity.

[1] Colin E. Gunton, 𝑇ℎ𝑒 𝑇𝑟𝑖𝑢𝑛𝑒 𝐶𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟: 𝐴 𝐻𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑜𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙 𝐴𝑛𝑑 𝑆𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑐 𝑆𝑡𝑢𝑑𝑦 (Grand Rapids, Michigan: William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 1998), Loc 1581, 1587 kindle.

LANSING, Mich. – The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) has expanded efforts to help reduce lead exposure to all eligible Michigan families through the Get Ahead of Lead initiative.

Now being offered to all communities, the Statewide Filter Support Program provides free certified lead-reducing drinking water filters and replacement cartridges to eligible households. Households qualify if a child under 19 on Medicaid or a pregnant Medicaid enrollee lives in the home and the home has, or may have: Lead or galvanized plumbing.

Lead exposure can come from a variety of sources, including paint in homes built before 1978, household dust, soil, drinking water from older plumbing, certain jobs and hobbies and some imported goods. Lead exposure can affect learning, behavior, growth and development in children, making prevention an important part of protecting family health.

Parents and caregivers of young children should also talk with their child’s health care provider about blood lead testing, especially if there is concern about possible exposure.

TOM: full details and context matters and they destroy the  false narrative
presented :

 This post refers to Canadian actress and entrepreneur Jasmine Mooney—but the headline strips away important context.

Mooney previously held a TN work visa, but U.S. border officials revoked it in November 2024. Mooney said officials questioned whether her paperwork was properly prepared and whether her work for a hemp-infused beverage company qualified.
On March 3, 2025, she approached the San Ysidro port of entry from Mexico with a new job offer and attempted to obtain new TN status.
Border officials denied her application. ICE stated that she was detained because she lacked legal documentation permitting her to enter or remain in the United States—not because she was Canadian and not because she had committed a violent crime.
She was held for 12 days and returned to Canada on March 15. She was not criminally charged.
“Wrapped in chains for 24 hours” was Mooney’s description of the restraints used while she and approximately 30 other detainees were transported from California to an Arizona detention facility. It does not mean agents literally wound chains around her continuously as punishment. The treatment and lengthy detention may reasonably be questioned, but the wording is sensationalized.
Importantly, Canadian citizenship does not create an automatic right to enter or work in the United States. A traveler may apply for TN status at a port of entry, but approval and admission are not guaranteed.

The accurate summary is: A Canadian citizen whose earlier work authorization had been revoked was denied new TN status, detained during immigration processing, restrained during an extended transfer, and returned to Canada after 12 days. The post presents her immigration detention as though ICE inexplicably seized a fully authorized Canadian traveler.

Sources: USCIS—TN status for Canadian and Mexican professionals⁠, CBS News—ICE’s stated reason for detention⁠, KGTV investigation and Mooney’s account⁠, NPR follow-up⁠.

text:
Kennedy Urlacher forced a safety for USC tonight.

He's a junior, he plays for one of the most famous programs in America, and he came out of high school in Arizona with 20 scholarship offers. Notre Dame, Penn State, Miami, TCU, Kansas State. He picked Notre Dame, then transferred to USC.

His father got one offer. Total.

Brian Urlacher's parents separated when he was young. His mother Lavoyda moved him and his siblings to Lovington, New Mexico, an oil town out near the Texas line, and worked several jobs at once to keep them afloat.

As a high school sophomore he was 5-foot-9 and 160 pounds, playing wide receiver.

Then he grew seven inches and gained 40 pounds in two years.

By his senior year he was 6-foot-4 and playing everywhere. Receiver, running back, kick returner, defensive back. He made All-State on both sides of the ball and led Lovington to a 14-0 season and the state championship back in 1995.

His assistant coach, Jaime Quinones, dragged him into the weight room and got him doing 5 a.m. workouts.

"Like a father-figure to me football-wise," Urlacher later called him.

What he wanted was Texas Tech. Lubbock was close, it was the program he'd grown up watching, and he went to their summer camps trying to get noticed.

He won MVP of their camp.

They never offered him.

Nobody else came either. Recruiters don't drive to Lovington. His mother couldn't pay for college without a scholarship.

The only offer he got was from the University of New Mexico, nine hours away.

He took it, and then barely played for two years. Special teams as a freshman, backup linebacker as a sophomore.

Then Rocky Long took over as head coach and stuck him at a hybrid safety and linebacker spot the Lobos called Lobo Back.

As a junior, Urlacher led the entire country in tackles and set a school record.

As a senior he was a consensus All-American, Mountain West Player of the Year, a Jim Thorpe Award finalist, and finished 12th in the Heisman voting.

Chicago took him ninth overall in 2000.

Defensive Rookie of the Year that season. Defensive Player of the Year in 2005. Eight Pro Bowls. Four times First Team All-Pro. 1,361 tackles. Hall of Fame on the first ballot.

His number 44 hangs retired in Albuquerque. Lovington named their high school football field after him.

One offer.

Now his kid plays in the Coliseum, and every school in the country wanted him.

text:
Senator Kelly has discovered the oldest trick in political theater: find a heartbreaking case, omit the eligibility details that determine the case, then cue the ominous music and blame every Republican from here to Wall Street.

The woman he cites reportedly works about 60 hours a month and says a disability makes working more difficult. That is precisely why the relevant question is not “Can we produce a sympathetic anecdote?” It is: Was she properly evaluated for a disability-based exemption, and was she offered the appeal and documentation process she is entitled to? USDA guidance says people unable to work because of a physical or mental limitation are excused from the ABAWD work requirement and its time limit. If she was wrongly denied that exemption, then the failure is an administrative determination worth correcting—not proof that Republicans declared war on disabled people.

And yes, for non-exempt ABAWD recipients, the standard is 80 hours per month—roughly 20 hours a week—not 60. Arizona has long described the relevant threshold as 20 hours weekly or an average of 80 hours monthly, including combinations of paid work, volunteering, or qualifying activities. The policy can be debated. But calling a known eligibility rule “Republicans cut food assistance” is a bit like calling a speed limit “Republicans banned driving.”

What Kelly leaves out:

Disability is not automatically the same as a SNAP work-rule exemption. The operative issue is whether the person is deemed unable to work under the program’s standards and has the required verification. That distinction is bureaucratic, imperfect, and often frustrating—but it is central, not a footnote.

The 80-hour rule is not simply “work or starve.”USDA says qualifying hours can include work, work programs, or a combination of both; Arizona similarly lists paid work, self-employment, volunteering, and in-kind work among qualifying activities.

Kelly’s own account does not establish the cause of the denial. His press release says the woman had filed four applications and encountered repeated difficulties getting an interview. That sounds at least partly like an access-and-administration problem. A senator could spend his energy demanding prompt interviews, competent case review, and proper disability-exemption screening—instead of treating incomplete paperwork or a stalled appointment as conclusive evidence of a billionaire-funded famine plot.

“Tax cuts for billionaires” is a political conclusion, not a caseworker’s explanation. The tax-and-spending law contains multiple provisions, and whether its overall distribution is fair is a legitimate political argument. But it does not magically answer whether this particular applicant was exempt, documented her limitation, received a timely interview, or was denied incorrectly.

The precise point

A responsible critique of the policy would say: expanding the 80-hour requirement and narrowing some exemptions can put vulnerable people at risk, especially when state agencies make it hard to navigate the process. That is a serious argument.

Kelly instead sells a cleaner, more useful campaign version: a disabled worker misses an eligibility threshold; therefore, Republicans personally took groceries from her cart to hand champagne to a billionaire. It is rhetorically efficient—facts, after all, are so much less photogenic than a villain monologue.

If this constituent truly cannot work enough hours because of a qualifying medical limitation, she should be screened for the exemption, helped with documentation, and given access to an appeal. That would be governing. Posting a moral panic around an unresolved individual eligibility case is content creation.

TRIGGER WARNING: This story discusses suicide and the death of a young person.

CBI REVIEW UPHOLDS SUICIDE FINDING IN DEATH OF CU BOULDER STUDENT MEGAN TRUSSELL

The Colorado Bureau of Investigation has completed an independent state-level review into the 2025 death of 18-year-old CU Boulder student Megan Trussell, concluding there is no evidence supporting homicide or physical assault and upholding the original determination that she died by suicide.

Trussell disappeared in February 2025 while attending the University of Colorado Boulder. Her body was found in Boulder Canyon approximately one week after she was last seen.

The independent review was initiated in January at the request of the Trussell family and conducted under the authority of Colorado Senate Bill 22-150.

According to CBI, the review lasted roughly seven months and included examination of the investigative record, digital evidence, cellular analysis, campus records, body-camera footage, search efforts and forensic files.

The case was also presented July 21 to CBI's Cold Case Review Team, a group of approximately 40 professionals that includes law enforcement personnel, forensic experts, toxicologists and victim advocates. A letter from the Trussell family was read to the team as part of the process.

CBI said its review found no evidence supporting homicide or physical assault and identified no incomplete investigative step that would change the original conclusion that Trussell's death was a suicide.

Medical experts who participated in the review also supported the coroner's findings. According to CBI, toxicology results showing elevated amphetamine levels and physical evidence of severe hypothermic exposure were consistent with the original cause-of-death findings.

The review also examined the initial search for Trussell.

CBI concluded that the response by the Boulder County Sheriff's Office and its partner agencies was reasonable and substantial, noting that search operations were expanded despite difficult terrain, snowfall and extreme cold that limited visibility and affected the use of dog teams and drones in Boulder Canyon.

"Based on the totality of the record, and with input from Cold Case Review Team experts, the CBI concluded that the original response and investigation by the Boulder County Sheriff's Office and partner agencies were reasonable, substantial and supported by the available evidence," CBI stated.

CBI Director Armando Saldate III acknowledged that the review cannot resolve every question for Trussell's family.

"No administrative review can undo the profound loss experienced by the Trussell family or answer every remaining question," Saldate said. "However, this statutory process ensures that every piece of evidence was examined with the utmost seriousness, rigor, and respect."

Saldate said CBI offered its findings with "deep compassion for Megan's grieving loved ones and a commitment to continuous improvement in law enforcement practices."

The state review ultimately found no evidence that would change the original determination surrounding Trussell's death.

If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

𝗦𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘆𝗲𝗱 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝘂𝗯𝘀 & 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗨𝗦 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀

The heavy green survey clusters reveal the operational math behind submarine routing. Vast stretches of the seas near the Chinese coast are too shallow for safe heavy submarine navigation. Conversely, deep trenches, troughs, and basins offer ideal environments for covert movement, hibernation, and acoustic hiding.

𝗠𝗮𝗷𝗼𝗿 𝗛𝘂𝗯𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀:

𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗺 & 𝗔𝗽𝗿𝗮 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗿: The anchor of U.S. submarine operations in the Western Pacific.

𝗝𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗪𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Heavily clustered areas in the Sea of Japan, east of the South Korean coast near Busan and Jinhae, east of Hokkaido, and east of Tokyo Bay beyond the deep Japan Trench.

𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽-𝗦𝗲𝗮 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 & 𝗥𝗶𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘀: Extensive mapping covers the Mariana Trench, Mariana Trough, West Mariana Ridge with Guam and Palau as the focal hubs, and the deep Java Trench.

Regional Chokepoints: Dense clusters wrap all around Guam and Palau, the vast seas between Okinawa and Luzon, and along the Bashi Channel heading toward Kaohsiung and the Batanes Islands.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗪𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗻

Submarines require specific minimum depths to safely navigate and avoid grounding, which rules out shallow continental shelves near mainland Asia. Conversely, deep trenches and basins provide superior thermal layers, complex acoustic clutter, and deep-water resting/hibernating zones where submarines can hold out with minimal risk of detection by Chinese surface anti-submarine warfare (ASW) assets and sensor grids.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗮 𝗛𝘂𝗯𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗨.𝗦. 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁

To sustain these operational corridors, a robust network of forward-deployed infrastructure supports U.S. and allied subsurface forces:

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: Operational control is anchored by U.S. Pacific Fleet (PACFLT) in Hawaii, U.S. Seventh Fleet headquartered at Yokosuka (Japan), and Submarine Group 7, which exercises operational command over all Western Pacific deployed submarines.

𝗝𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗻 & 𝗢𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘄𝗮: U.S. Fleet Activities Yokosuka serves as the primary headquarters for the U.S. Seventh Fleet and provides critical pier-side berthing and heavy repair capabilities via the Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Center (SRF-JRMC) for visiting and forward-stationed submarines. Sasebo provides supplementary logistics. While Okinawa (such as White Beach Naval Facility) hosts regular transient visits and expeditionary submarine support, nuclear submarines are heavily serviced out of main hubs.

𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗺 (𝗡𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗹 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗺 / 𝗔𝗽𝗿𝗮 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗿): Home to Submarine Squadron 15, Guam hosts permanently forward-deployed Los Angeles-class attack submarines alongside specialized submarine tenders (like the USS Emory S. Land and USS Frank Cable) that supply mobile maintenance, re-arming, and heavy repair capability directly in theater.

𝗧𝗮𝗶𝘄𝗮𝗻: While Taiwan does not host U.S. homeported submarines, its internal infrastructure is vital. Kaohsiung (specifically the Zuoying Naval Base) houses Taiwan's largest naval and submarine fleet headquarters. The close proximity of surveyed deep channels like the Bashi Channel ensures seamless tactical integration and operational synchronization between allied forces.

Carnival Cruise Line: The Complete Guide

Carnival Cruise Line is the world's largest cruise brand by passenger volume and is widely known as "America's Cruise Line." Founded in 1972 by entrepreneur Ted Arison, Carnival transformed cruising from an exclusive luxury vacation into an affordable, fun-filled getaway for families, couples, and groups of friends.

History and Evolution

Carnival Cruise Line began operations on March 11, 1972, with a single ship, the Mardi Gras, sailing from Miami. Ted Arison's vision was simple: make cruising accessible to ordinary travelers rather than only the wealthy.

Major milestones include:

1972 – Carnival founded by Ted Arison.
1982 – Introduction of Tropicale, Carnival's first purpose-built cruise ship.
1984 – First cruise line to advertise on network television, featuring Kathie Lee Gifford.
1987 – Carnival becomes the world's most popular cruise line by passenger volume.
1996 – Introduction of Carnival Destiny, the first passenger ship to exceed 100,000 gross tons.
2021 – Launch of Mardi Gras, the first cruise ship in North America powered by LNG and the first cruise ship with a roller coaster at sea.

Today Carnival operates nearly 30 ships and carries millions of guests annually.

The "Fun Ship" Concept

Perhaps no cruise line has marketed itself more successfully than Carnival with its famous**"Fun Ship"** slogan.

The term reflects Carnival's philosophy that a cruise should be:

Casual rather than formal
Family-friendly
Activity-packed
Affordable
Social and energetic
Entertainment-focused

The Fun Ship concept emphasizes pool parties, comedy clubs, waterparks, music, games, family activities, and nightlife rather than the traditional image of formal ocean travel. Carnival later expanded this philosophy with initiatives such as "Fun Ship 2.0" and "Choose Fun."

Shaquille O'Neal has become one of the company's most visible modern spokespeople through television commercials, social media campaigns, and onboard events.

Repeat Guest Loyalty

Carnival's VIFP (Very Important Fun Person) Club is one of the largest cruise loyalty programs in the industry.

A precise Carnival-wide percentage of guests who book another Carnival cruise is not publicly disclosed in the sources reviewed. However, Carnival consistently emphasizes repeat business and loyalty as major drivers of its success, and millions of guests return to sail with the company multiple times. Carnival also reported attracting over 3.5 million first-time cruisers in 2023, expanding its future loyalty base.

Because Carnival does not publicly publish an official fleet-wide repeat-booking percentage, any exact number often quoted online should be viewed cautiously unless directly sourced from the company.

Bottom Line

Carnival Cruise Line built its reputation by making cruising affordable, energetic, and family-friendly. Its "Fun Ship" philosophy, extensive fleet, numerous embarkation ports, broad destination network, excellent children's programming, and relatively affordable pricing continue to make it one of the most popular vacation brands in the world. Whether you're a first-time cruiser or a seasoned passenger, Carnival remains one of the strongest value propositions in mainstream cruising.

text:
Happy 87th Birthday to George Lazenby

Born | September 5, 1939 in Goulburn, New South Wales, Australia

George Lazenby Trivia

• Bond producer Albert R. Broccoli remarked that Lazenby could have been the best Bond had he not quit after just one film.

• He was offered a seven-movie deal by the Bond producers, but quit the role because he felt that the tuxedo-clad Bond would die out in the new hippie culture that had permeated society in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

• Later regretted leaving the Bond series after just one film. He claimed he listened to bad advice.

• He is estimated to be the wealthiest actor to have played James Bond.

• He says that his favourite Bond film is Goldfinger (1964).

• He was the youngest actor to play James Bond, being 30 when On Her Majesty's Secret Service (1969) was released.

• Was a personal-combat instructor in the Australian Special Forces; he has black belts in Judo, Shotokan-Ryu Karate, and Jeet-Kune-Do, having studied martial arts under Bruce Lee himself.

• He was a close personal friend of Bruce Lee. He met Lee in 1972 and the two became fast friends. Lazenby studied Lee's personal martial arts and philosophical teaching of Jeet Kune Do under Lee until the time of Lee's death in 1973. Lazenby was actually going to have dinner with Bruce Lee the night he died. Lazenby would later say that it was Lee's teachings that allowed him to go on to have such a successful business career and personal life.

• His agent, Maggie Smith, told him that he should apply for Bond, since in her opinion, his arrogance would surely win him the role.

• Was the #1 male fashion model in the world from 1964 to 1968.

• Served as a sergeant in the Australian Special Forces.

• Broke a stuntman's nose during a Bond fight screen test, and it was this physical strength that finalised his selection as Bond.

• He holds the unique distinction of having been both The Marlboro Man and James Bond, as he played 007 in one film and was also the European Marlboro Man.

• This makes Lazenby the actor that first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond and also the actor that first replaced Bruce Lee as Golden Harvest's martial arts action hero after Lee's death. Many subsequent actors would then follow Lazenby playing Bond as well as imitating Bruce Lee.

• He owns mansions in Hawaii, Brentwood, California, Australia; and a 600 acre estate/ranch in Valyermo, Los Angeles County, California.

• Is an accomplished skier and in fact had won two skiing contests in Australia before becoming James Bond.

• Was the highest paid male model in Europe prior to playing James Bond.

• Lived in drummer for The Who ― Keith Moon's famous London Waterhouse complete with Hydro Hovercraft that came right into the living room through the front door, for a period of 6 months in the late '60s.

• He is the only actor, other than Sean Connery, to play James Bond to have served in the military and the only one to have served in any branch of the Special Forces as Bond did.

text:
This bloke says he served in the Royal Navy for 11 years and now supports Reform UK. Just how stupid/gullible/radicalised is he? 

His dumb central claim is completely false: work visas carry a "No Recourse to Public Funds" condition.

Skilled Worker visas, Health and Care Worker visas, and the family visas used to bring dependants over are all listed by the Home Office as subject to a Home Office imposed condition of no access to public funds.

That means someone here on a work visa cannot claim most benefits, tax credits or housing assistance that are paid by the state, including income support, income-based jobseeker's allowance, universal credit, working tax credit, housing and homelessness assistance, and carer's allowance.

So his tweet's whole premise (visa holder arrives, brings family, "benefits paid") inverts reality. The default position is the opposite of your bullshit claim.

Also:

"Brings over their mum, dad, brother, sister"

UK family visa rules don't generally permit bringing over parents or adult siblings on a work visa's dependant route; the family visa system is mainly for spouses/partners and children under 18, and even those dependants inherit the NRPF condition unless it is removed in limited circumstances.

"No nationality check, no status check, no face-to-face assessment"

He offers zero evidence in support of this and it contradicts how DWP claims actually work: Universal Credit and other claims require identity verification and immigration status checks precisely because of the NRPF rule. 

The DWP has to establish someone isn't subject to it before paying anything.

The framing is classic 'JAQing off in public' (like his hero dodgy spiv Farage does all the fucking time), a textbook "just asking questions" move: present a fabricated process as established fact, then dare "any Tory, or anyone on the left" to defend it.

It's not inviting debate, it's a combination of fallacious argumentation, misleading disinformation, and shameless lying achieved through asserting a falsehood, and then demanding people justify something that doesn't happen.

text:
“Give Investigators Space”: Why Volunteer Searchers Say Sheriff Chris Nanos Shut Them Out of the Nancy Guthrie Search

Missing Lost And Trafficked 
Lured Lost And Unsolved 

TUCSON, Ariz. — As the search for Nancy Guthrie stretched into its fifth month, a disputes have  erupted over who was allowed to look for her on the ground. Public statements from the Pima County Sheriff’s Department show that officials asked private volunteer search groups to step back and leave the work to professionals. 

Separately, the United Cajun Navy says Sheriff Chris Nanos’s office repeatedly rejected  offers of trained search-and-rescue assistance, including K-9 and drone teams.

What the sheriff’s department said

On Feb. 21, the Pima County Sheriff’s Department addressed “private search parties” in a three-part public statement. The department said volunteer groups had inquired about operating in the area and that, “Per the Sheriff,” they had been asked to give investigators room to work. The statement added that the search was “best left to professionals,” directed interested people toward volunteer opportunities with the department, and reminded the public that property owners control access to private land. 

“We appreciate their concern, and we all want to find Nancy, but this work is best left to professionals.” — Pima County Sheriff’s Department, as quoted by Newsweek and FOX 10 Phoenix. 

The department’s position came as investigators continued to process evidence and review surveillance footage. Newsweek reported that new barricades were placed near Guthrie’s home amid the presence of news crews, true-crime observers and other members of the public. 

 FOX 10 Phoenix reported that detectives were continuing neighborhood canvassing and that the department had collected multiple gloves and other items for analysis. 

From the department’s perspective, the instruction was not presented as a prohibition on all community assistance. Rather, officials said that people who wanted to help should use official channels, respect private-property boundaries and avoid interfering with an active investigation. That distinction matters: the public statement documents a request to step back from independent searches, not a published countywide order making all civilian searches unlawful.

What happened when volunteers searched anyway

The dispute became more concrete when a group of volunteers from Mexico conducted an independent search near Guthrie’s Tucson neighborhood. FOX 10 reported that members of the group, which is associated with the Searching Mothers of Sonora, found a black glove and a backpack several miles from Guthrie’s home. Deputies took possession of the backpack, and the station reported that some volunteers had also been looking around the front yard of Guthrie’s residence. 

That episode illustrates why law-enforcement agencies often seek to control a crime scene and surrounding search areas. An object found by civilians may be unrelated, may carry contamination from multiple people, or may require documentation about where and how it was located before it can be evaluated as evidence. In this case, FOX 10 cited a genetic genealogist who questioned whether the glove was likely to yield a usable investigative profile, while also reporting that PCSD was analyzing evidence and would not publicly disclose detailed forensic information during the active investigation. [3]

The volunteer group’s actions, however, also show the source of public frustration. With Guthrie still missing and official updates limited, some community members concluded that additional eyes on the ground could help. The department’s answer was that unauthorized searching risked crowding investigators and complicating the evidentiary picture.

The United Cajun Navy’s allegation

The most direct allegation that professional outside assistance was blocked came from Brian Trascher, vice president of the United Cajun Navy. In a June 30 interview reported by NewsNation, Trascher said the organization made multiple offers to assist and submitted a detailed plan to Nanos. He said the plan contemplated K-9 teams, drones and partner organizations capable of conducting searches near the U.S.-Mexico border. [4]

Trascher characterized the decision as a “blanket” refusal by the sheriff’s office to accept outside help. He said the organization believed a border-area search was worth pursuing and that early assistance would have been especially valuable. Entertainment Weekly published a similar account, quoting Trascher’s description of the proposed resources and reporting that the sheriff’s office did not immediately respond to the outlet’s request for comment. [4] [5]

The United Cajun Navy’s account is significant because it concerns a group that describes itself as providing disaster response, humanitarian aid and search-and-rescue services, rather than merely unaffiliated members of the public. But the account remains an allegation by the organization’s representative. The NewsNation and Entertainment Weekly reports establish that the offer was made and that Trascher says it was rejected; they do not, by themselves, establish the precise internal decision-making process, whether conditions were attached to the offer, or whether every outside professional group was denied access in every location.

MONEY-HUNGRY INSURANCE COMPANIES!!!  UnitedHealthcare told a South Carolina mom her son's brain rehab is "not medically necessary" after he woke up from a crash!!
⠀
Peyton Alvarez, 25, a PSA Airlines mechanic, hit a tree on Perimeter Road in Greenville on April 28. He had a helmet on and still took a traumatic brain injury. Doctors told his mother, Trina, he might never wake up.
⠀
He stayed unconscious for weeks. In June he opened an eye, moved an arm, and wiggled his toes. Shepherd Center in Atlanta accepted him for specialized rehab. The family had the ambulance booked.
⠀
On July 7 UnitedHealthcare denied it. The letter called the transfer "not medically necessary" and offered a skilled nursing facility instead. Trina and his doctors appealed. The company upheld the denial.
⠀
UnitedHealthcare put this in writing: a doctor's order "does not, in itself, make" the treatment medically necessary. The rehab center will not take cash. Without the insurer, he does not go.
⠀
"It makes me so angry that they can control what happens with my son," Trina said. "The longer he stays at the hospital he's at, the less chance he has to wake up."
⠀
This is the business model. KFF found ACA Marketplace plans denied 18 percent of standard prior-auth requests in 2025. UnitedHealth denied 21 percent on those exchanges and 17 percent in Medicare Advantage, the highest among the big MA insurers KFF measured.
⠀
A federal watchdog found UnitedHealth denied inpatient rehab requests 66 percent of the time in Medicare Advantage post-hospital cases. When people appeal, a huge share of those denials get overturned. Most families never appeal.
⠀
Obama's Affordable Care Act did not invent prior authorization. It did lock private insurers in as the gatekeepers of the exchanges, then let them keep 15 to 20 percent under the medical-loss-ratio rule while they scaled Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care.

UnitedHealth bought NaviHealth for $1.1 billion to run post-acute denials with an algorithm. Congress is still asking why doctors lose to that stack.
⠀⠀

text: The spectacle unfolding in Plymouth is not merely a local trial dispute. It is a cultural rewrite of a principle that has stood, with only rare and tightly cabined exceptions, for a quarter of a millennium of American law: a single juror may refuse to surrender a verdict he or she does not believe, and that refusal is not a defect to be cured but a feature of the system. Consider the counterfactual. In rural Alabama in 1951 a Black defendant stands accused of raping a white woman. Eleven jurors are eager to convict and send him to the penitentiary for decades. One juror holds out. The result is a mistrial. Commentators in Connecticut, New York, and Massachusetts would have called that lone holdout an American hero—the last remaining check against a majority determined to impose its will regardless of reasonable doubt. The same commentators would have denounced any attempt to identify, isolate, or remove that juror as an assault on the independence the Constitution assigns to the jury box. Today the geography and the identities are reversed, and so is the rhetoric. In Plymouth the holdout is spoken of with visible contempt: “He was a man.” The phrase is not offered as demographic description. It is offered as accusation. Emotion has displaced the settled rule that a deliberating juror may be discharged only for reasons personal to that juror and wholly unrelated to the evidence or to disagreement with fellow jurors. Reasonable doubt is not a group project. Once a holdout is publicly branded a problem, the pressure leaves the jury room and becomes a spectacle. A mistrial is an honest, if inconvenient, result. Coercing unanimity is not. The principle does not change with the defendant, the venue, or the political valence of the case. If it did, it was never a principle.

text:
Tom Cruise was 23 when he found himself acting opposite Paul Newman in The Color of Money.

Having your lines memorized is one thing. Delivering them opposite one of Hollywood’s greatest actors is another.

Cruise admitted he was intimidated.

Newman was 61, had already earned nearly every kind of admiration Hollywood could offer and had those eyes just to make the situation completely unreasonable.

But what Newman taught Cruise away from the cameras is what made me love this story.

Newman put him at ease and welcomed him into his life beyond the set. He introduced Cruise to auto racing and invited him to his home in Connecticut.

Cruise later called Newman a role model, and it was not simply because of his acting.

He watched how Newman worked, how he treated people and how he carried himself when no camera was pointed at him.

I like that kind of mentoring. No grand speech required. No leather chair beside a fireplace.

Newman simply let a young actor see what decades of talent, discipline and decency looked like up close.

Cruise arrived expecting to learn from Paul Newman, the actor.

What stayed with him was Paul Newman, the man.

text:
A mysterious character known as the "Leatherman" wandered a 365-mile route in the 1800s without any clear reason. His real name, origins, or the purpose of his travels remained unknown, yet he became a beloved local figure.

Dressed in a heavy outfit crafted from old leather boots and ties, weighing over 60 pounds, the Leatherman braved all weather conditions and seasons. He was so punctual in his travels between the Hudson and Connecticut rivers, covering 40 small towns every 34 days, that locals could tell the time by his location. He famously slept in caves, maintaining a strict schedule.

The Leatherman communicated little, only making a few sounds in English or French, but was warmly anticipated in each town he visited. Being visited by him was seen as an honor, and children were eager to offer him food during his stops.

After his death, the Leatherman's grave became a site of interest, leading to its relocation by a historical society to prevent accidents. In 2011, an attempt to uncover his identity through DNA testing failed when it was discovered his remains were gone, deepening the mystery around him.

See more: https://t.co/FRrL4hIDpN

Chanticleers-Mountaineers Total Edge

With Coastal Carolina heading to Morgantown to face West Virginia, the betting market is showing some interesting hesitation on the total. We are looking at a line hovering around 54.5 to 55, and there is a clear opportunity to capitalize on the current pricing.

West Virginia enters this season opener with a lot of hype surrounding their new-look offense, particularly with Mike Hawkins Jr. taking the reins at quarterback. While the Mountaineers are heavy favorites, season openers often feature a bit of "feeling out" time for new coaching staffs and personnel. Coastal Carolina is also breaking in a new era under Ryan Beard, and while they have a history of being competitive, integrating a new defensive scheme on the road against a Power conference opponent usually leads to a more conservative, controlled game plan rather than a high-scoring shootout.

The current odds on Kalshi offer a nice look at the Under 55 at -104. Given that West Virginia is expected to dictate the pace and likely won't need to keep their foot on the gas for all four quarters if they build an early lead, the Under feels like the sharper play. We aren't expecting a defensive struggle, but we are betting against the game turning into a track meet.

Pick: Under 55 (-104 on Kalshi)

THE COLD READ
A Guru Nanga tale, 26 of 33

14. MONTESSORI TO EIGHTH GRADE, MAKER VOCATIONAL HIGH SCHOOL, TWO YEARS OF SERVICE, THEN FREE TUITION THROUGH THE PHD

The roommate had folded his arms, in the way of a man who has already chosen a track and would like to hear it defended.

"This item is four proposals in a trench coat," said Guru Nanga. "Guru Nanga will take them in order, and then he will take the trench coat."

"Montessori. Across thirty-two studies, it shows an effect of about a quarter of a standard deviation on academics and a third on everything else. That is real. It comes from families who chose it, only 48.8 percent of the randomized treatment group stayed through kindergarten, and the effect is strongest in preschool and weakest in the very middle-school years the list would mandate. California does not recognize the credential, so the state would be mandating a method it cannot staff. Offer Montessori as a choice inside every district and license the teachers. Do not require it of a fourteen-year-old who wants a chemistry lab."

"Vocational high school. The record likes this and asks for a hyphen. Career academies raised earnings by about eleven percent over eight years in a randomized trial of 1,764 students, and California's Linked Learning pathways point the same way. But across eighteen countries, the employment advantage of a purely vocational track reverses around age fifty, worst in the countries that do it best. Teach the trade with the algebra, not instead of it. As for 'Maker skills,' the whole research base is twenty-two studies and no pooled effect. Guru Nanga has made things. He recommends it. He cannot yet cite it."

The roommate unfolded his arms.

Luke said nothing. Guru Nanga noted it. Listening is acknowledged, not cited, and that is the correct order of the two.

"Two years of compulsory service. A state cannot conscript. The war power that let the federal government do it in 1918 is a federal power. France announced universal national service and it became a voluntary twelve-day stay with no sanction for skipping it. When Germany ended conscription, the civilian service that had quietly staffed its hospitals collapsed from ninety thousand a year to seventeen thousand three hundred volunteers, of whom three thousand were new. A mandate that cannot be enforced is a suggestion with a uniform."

text:
THE COLD READ
A Guru Nanga tale, 25 of 33

13. IMMIGRATION FAVORING UNSKILLED LABOR; RAPIDLY EXPAND LEGAL LABOR

The roommate asked this one on behalf of his family.

"Guru Nanga will begin with the law, because it is short. In 2012 the Supreme Court held that immigration is a federal system, 'a single integrated and all-embracing system,' and struck down most of Arizona's attempt to run its own. A state does not have an immigration policy. It has an opinion about one. This is not a criticism of the idea. It is a description of the building it lives in."

"So does everyone in this park," said Luke.

"Then the state can do nothing?" said the roommate.

"The state can do the thing nobody does. The federal farmworker visa, H-2A, has no cap. None. Fifty-six percent of California farmers say they cannot hire enough workers, and under six percent use the visa. Certified positions rose eight hundred percent in a decade, from 4,505 to 40,758, and the constraint is still cost, housing, and paperwork. Britain offered fifty-seven thousand seasonal visas in 2023 and issued 32,724. Supply of visas is not the constraint. The transaction cost of using one is. The word in the list that fails is 'rapidly.' Canada's provincial nominee program is the model that works, and it works slowly, by design, with the federal government holding the pen."

Luke asked about wages, because the roommate would not.

"The National Academies' synthesis finds immigration raises the relative wages of American-born workers without a high-school diploma slightly, about a third of a percent, and lowers those of earlier immigrants by about three and a half. When the Bracero program ended in 1964, farm wages in the exposed states did not rise faster than elsewhere; growers bought machines. The record does not support the fear. It does not support the euphoria either. It supports paperwork reform, which has never once been on a bumper sticker."

"It wouldn't fit," said Luke.

The finding: ask Congress for a state-nominee visa on the Canadian model, with California nominating and Washington deciding. Meanwhile, build a state office that files H-2A on behalf of small growers, fronts the housing, and makes the visa portable between employers so a worker can leave a bad one. Strike the word 'rapidly.' Replace it with a fiscal year.

First the CIA director flies in. He makes threats. He’s told, in so many words, to go fuck himself. Next comes a show of escalation — during which the United States sits quietly in the shadows and gives its European marionettes room to throw a fit, those same marionettes who still sincerely believe they are sovereign. After that, the familiar negotiators arrive.

The West operates by the models of social psychology — universal only in part, because everything they rest on was researched in the West, on Western subjects — and assumes Russia is not all that different and will react according to the patterns and rules they have identified.

With an individual, especially a young one driven into a corner, that might work. With grown people here, with Russian tempering, and still more with a state system made of such people, it does not.

Meanwhile, coercive diplomacy is unfolding in plain sight. Good cop, bad cop. The bad cop has already been here. Now two nice guys — the ones the chebureks in Zaryadye have been waiting for — have landed in Moscow.

The scheme, the hard-power version of the door-in-the-face technique, looks like this in its pure form:

Threat + unacceptable terms → refusal → escalation → negotiators (creating the illusion of an “exit” from a supposedly hopeless situation).
Against the backdrop of pressure already applied, the deal is meant, in the manipulators’ design, to look like their concession and our salvation — not like capitulation from a standing start. And each round, run in cycles, makes that “exit” narrower and more inconvenient.

The key nuance without which the scheme fails: it is not enough for the one making threats to frighten you. He also has to offer a credible guarantee that, if you agree, the pressure will stop and there will be an “honest peace.”

Will the current visit produce any diplomatic movement? Of course not. Talking to Russia from a position of strength is useless. What does a Russian do when the other side starts acting the bull? Either he tries to get rid of the nuisance — or he hits him in the face.

Even if the West wanted to talk differently, it no longer has that option. Today’s militarism and hysteria have cut it off: if it starts that game now, its rabid hangers-on will accuse the ruling elites of betrayal, defeatism, and whatever other sins are known only to them.

The West’s bet on intimidation only kills any desire to talk at all, to hear anything coming from that direction, let alone to listen.

There is little point to what is happening beyond giving Ukraine a few days to regroup during the white gentlemen’s tour, so it can continue state terrorism — “raising the stakes to force peace,” as Kiev’s handlers like to put it.

You’re mixing up two different things.
Those 12 million Germans were Germans. After a war Germany started, they were pushed out of Poland, Czechoslovakia, and other places the Allies redrew. Then Germany took them in—same people, same language, a state that still existed and treated them as its own. They became citizens there. Nobody kept their grandchildren as “refugees” for 75 years with a UN agency and a claim to a house in Silesia. The file ended because their own nation-state absorbed them.

Palestine was not that. In 1948 it was a British Mandate, not a Palestinian country with a government and citizenship that could do what Germany did. The UN offered an Arab state and a Jewish state. Arab leaders rejected it. There was no Palestinian state to “rehome” anyone. What did exist were Arab states next door—Jordan, Egypt, Syria, Lebanon—same language, same religion. They could have done the German thing: take the displaced in as their people and close the file. Most of them didn’t. They kept people in camps and turned “return” into a demand that Israel stop existing.

So the comparison does not mean Israel had to take back a population whose leadership had just tried to prevent a Jewish state. The real parallel is: Germany absorbed Germans. Israel absorbed Jews thrown out of Arab countries. Arab states largely refused to absorb Palestinian Arabs as nationals. That’s why one refugee problem ended and this one was kept alive. Israel isn’t the villain for surviving a war and not undoing the outcome. The states that claimed to represent those refugees are the ones who chose camps over citizenship.

text:
Colonel Charles "Chargin' Charlie" Beckwith, the founder of America's Army SMU. Born in Atlanta in 1929, Beckwith was good enough at football to draw a draft offer from the Green Bay Packers in 1952, and turned it down to join the Army instead, choosing the fight in Korea over the one on the gridiron. He commissioned into the Infantry, served in Korea and later the 82nd Airborne, and graduated Ranger School in 1958, the launching point for a career that would reshape American special operations entirely.

The idea was born out of near-death. In the early 1960s, deployed to Malaya alongside the British SAS fighting a communist insurgency, Beckwith contracted leptospirosis, a brutal bacterial infection that doctors called one of the three worst cases they'd ever seen, giving him three weeks to live. He survived anyway. That time embedded with the SAS convinced him America needed its own version of that unit, and in 1963 he stood up Project Delta, hand-picking men for long-range reconnaissance work in Vietnam, where he was later shot in the abdomen with a .50-caliber round and survived that too.

It took until 1977 for his vision to become permanent, when Beckwith and Colonel Tom Henry formally established the unit, built directly on the SAS model, anti-terrorism, hostage rescue, and covert reconnaissance all rolled into one. He built its selection standard around what became known as the Long March, a brutal endurance test designed specifically to find men as tough, or tougher, than the SAS troopers who'd inspired the whole idea. The unit's first real mission came in April 1980, Operation Eagle Claw, the doomed attempt to rescue American hostages in Tehran, which ended in the Desert One disaster and the deaths of eight servicemen. Beckwith retired from the Army not long after, but the lessons from that failure directly led to the creation of the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment and, eventually, the entire joint special operations architecture the country still relies on today. A man nearly killed twice over who built the most storied special mission unit in American history anyway.
