545 vs. 300,000,000 People- by Charlie Reese

Politicians are the only people in the world who create problems and then campaign against them.

Have you ever wondered, if both the Democrats and the Republicans are against deficits, WHY do we have deficits?

Have you ever wondered, if all the politicians are against inflation and high taxes, WHY do we have inflation and high taxes?

You and I don't propose a federal budget. The President does.
You and I don't have the Constitutional authority to vote on appropriations.
The House of Representatives does.
You and I don't write the tax code, Congress does.
You and I don't set fiscal policy, Congress does.
You and I don't control monetary policy, the Federal Reserve Bank does.
One hundred senators, 435 congressmen, one President, and nine Supreme Court justices equates to 545 human beings out of the 300 million are directly, legally, morally, and individually responsible for the domestic problems that plague this country.
I excluded the members of the Federal Reserve Board because that problem was created by the Congress. In 1913, Congress delegated its Constitutional duty to provide a sound currency to a federally chartered, but private, central bank.
I excluded all the special interests and lobbyists for a sound reason. They have no legal authority. They have no ability to coerce a senator, a congressman, or a President to do one cotton-picking thing. I don't care if they offer a politician $1 million dollars in cash.
The politician has the power to accept or reject it. No matter what the lobbyist promises, it is the legislator's responsibility to determine how he votes.
Those 545 human beings spend much of their energy convincing you that what they did is not their fault. They cooperate in this common con regardless of party.
What separates a politician from a normal human being is an excessive amount of gall. No normal human being would have the gall of a Speaker, who stood up and criticized the President for creating deficits. The President can only propose a budget. He cannot force the Congress to accept it.
The Constitution, which is the supreme law of the land, gives sole responsibility to the House of Representatives for originating and approving appropriations and taxes.
Who is the speaker of the House now ? He is the leader of the majority party. He and fellow House members, not the President, can approve any budget they want. If the President vetoes it, they can pass it over his veto if they agree to.
It seems inconceivable to me that a nation of 300 million cannot replace 545 people who stand convicted -- by present facts -- of incompetence and irresponsibility. I can't think of a single domestic problem that is not traceable directly to those 545 people. When you fully grasp the plain truth that 545 people exercise the power of the federal government, then it must follow that what exists is what they want to exist.
If the tax code is unfair, it's because they want it unfair.
If the budget is in the red, it's because they want it in the red.
If the Army & Marines are in Iraq and Afghanistan it's because they want them in Iraq and Afghanistan ... If they do not receive social security but are on an elite retirement plan not available to the people, it's because they want it that way.
There are no insoluble government problems.
Do not let these 545 people shift the blame to bureaucrats, whom they hire and whose jobs they can abolish; to lobbyists, whose gifts and advice they can reject; to regulators, to whom they give the power to regulate and from whom they can take this power.
Above all, do not let them con you into the belief that there exists disembodied mystical forces like "the economy," "inflation," or "politics" that prevent them from doing what they take an oath to do.
Those 545 people, and they alone, are responsible.
They, and they alone, have the power. They, and they alone, should be held accountable by the people who are their bosses, provided the voters have the gumption to manage their own employees...
We should vote all of them out of office and clean up their mess!
What you do with this article now that you have read it... is up to you.
This might be funny if it weren't so true.
Be sure to read all the way to the end:
Tax his land,
Tax his bed,
Tax the table, at which he's fed.

Commemoration.

Prophet Zachariah and Elizabeth
Much of his story is told in the first chapter of Luke’s Gospel. The Synaxarion continues:

‘After the birth of Christ, Zacharias plainly declared the virginity of Mary and showed her truly to be the Mother of God; for he appointed her a place in that part of the Temple reserved for the virgins and so brought upon himself the hatred of the priests and levites.

‘When John was six months old, Zacharias hid him and his mother in a cave beyond the Jordan because King Herod, hearing of the birth in Bethlehem of the king of the Jews and fearing a rival of his own worldly power, sent soldiers to kill all the male children of Bethlehem. His enemies seized this opportunity to denounce Zacharias to Herod, who had him pursued and put to death within the precinct of the Temple, at the very place the Mother of God abode for a witnes to her virginity. As the Prophet’s blood flowed within the sanctuary, it signified the withdrawing of the divine Presence. Priests came to take up his body and they buried him with his fathers. From that moment signs and prodigies occurred in the Temple, indicating that the rites of the Law would soon be abolished. No longer would the priests behold the angels of God, or have the grace of prophecy; no longer would they be able to deliver oracles or enlighten the people upon the dark places of holy Scripture, as they had been wont to do.’

Holy Hieromartyr Athanasius of Brest-Litovsk (1649)
“Saint Athanasius was born in the province of Minsk in 1596, the same year as the false Union of Brest-Litovsk was concluded between Rome and some Russian bishops. His father was a Lithuanian nobleman of modest means, but Athanasius acquired a breadth and depth of learning that were exceptional at that time. Besides modern and ancient languages and the writings of the holy Fathers, he was familiar with the works of Western philosophers and theologians.

“In 1627, after spending several years as a private tutor, he became a monk at the Monastery of Khutyn near Orsha in Little Russia. This monastery was independent of the Polish occupying forces and, by tradition, deeply committed to the preservation of Orthodoxy, so that it was able to offer great encouragement to the Orthodox people in the face of Roman Catholic propaganda. Athanasius went on to follow his monastic path in other renowned monasteries, and was ordained priest. The Metropolitan of Kiev, Peter Moghila, gave him the task of restoring the Monastery of Kupyatitsk. In obedience to a divine revelation, Athanasius set out for Moscow, a long and dangerous journey through territory under Polish occupation, in order to ask for financial assistance for the restoration, and to acquaint the Tsar with the fate intended for the Orthodox Church in the lands to the south-west of Russia. He was successful in his quest and with the help of the Mother of God, the restoration works were begun. Two years later, Athanasius was appointed Abbot of the Monastery of St Symeon the Stylite in Brest-Litovsk. From then on, he was to be a resolute and tireless fighter against Roman proselytism, clothed in Orthodox rites and customs known as the Unia. For the next eight years, by prayer, preaching and through his writings, the Saint devoted all his strength to refuting the false Union, and to bringing back to the holy sheep-fold of Christ those who had strayed.

“The population of the occupied territories was brutally treated by the Polish soldiers and colonists, nor did the Jesuit missionaries, for their part, abstain from any measure that might serve to lead the peoples of Little Russia to accept their faith. In this situation, Saint Athanasius decided to petition the King of Poland, Vladislav IV, that the Orthodox be treated with more humanity. The King was moved by his request and issued a decree forbidding the abuses that had occurred, but his officials ignored it. The condition of the Orthodox in Warsaw was particularly bad. It was not unknown for the Poles and Uniates to set fire to Orthodox churches on feast days when they were full of the faithful, just as had happened in the time of the great Persecutions.

“Athanasius kept up the fight, aided and comforted by none but the Mother of God, and in 1643, following a new revelation, he again appealed for redress on behalf of the Orthodox to the Polish Council of State. He received a favourable hearing and the Orthodox were granted some legal protection. But certain Orthodox men of rank, fearing for their privileges, claimed that the Saint was mad and succeeded in having him deprived of his abbacy, deposed from the priesthood and sent to Kiev to answer before a church court.

“The humble Athanasius was completely exonerated and restored to his position, but he did not have peace for long, since persecution of the Orthodox soon began again. He drew up a petition intended for the King of Poland, but was arrested and thrown into prison before he was able to complete it. He was released after three years’ detention but, in 1648, a persecution broke out that was more terrible than ever before. So bloody was it that the people of Little Russia rose up and demanded the departure of the Polish-Lithuanian army and the restoration of Russian territory to the Tsar. The Polish authorities immediately arrested the rebel leaders and prominent Orthodox dignitaries. Saint Athanasius was imprisoned, and endured physical and mental torments of all kinds at the hands of his gaolers and of the Roman Catholic authorities, but he never ceased to cry, ‘Anathema to the Union!’ After being tortured with red-hot coals, he was flayed and burnt alive. As he was still not dead, his executioners shot him.

“They threw his decapitated corpse into a pit, where it was found some time later incorrupt. In the years that followed, the relics of the holy Martyr worked many miracles.” (Synaxarion)

Holy Martyrs Abda the bishop, Hormizd and Sunin of Persia (4th c)
Saint Abda lived in Persia during the reign of the Emperor Theodosius II and of the Persian king Yazgerd I; as bishop of the Christians there, he labored tirelessly to care for his own flock and bring the pagans to Christ. One day, full of zeal, he entered the temple at which the king made sacrifice, overturned the sacred fire and set the temple on fire. The enraged king forbade the worship of the Christian God, ordered the destruction of all the churches and monasteries, and arrested all of the clergy. Abda was brought before the king and ordered to rebuild the pagan temple; when he refused, he was cruelly and lengthily tortured until he gave up his soul to God. This was the beginning of a thirty-year period of terrible persecution for Christians in Persia.

Saint Hormizd was the son of a Persian governor who became a Christian in his youth. For this, his father condemned him to labor as a naked camel-herder in the desert. Some time later, the King sent Hormizd a linen tunic, promising to restore him to favor if he would return to the religion of the Persians. The Saint tore up the tunic and retured it to the king, for which he was executed.

Saint Sunin was a high Persian official who turned to Christ and was rewarded with a crown of martyrdom.

The Holy Martyrs Juventius and Maximinus
Little is known about the life of these two holy men, but their suffering for Christ is known from a sermon by St. John Chrysostom praising them. They were soldiers during the rule of Emperor Julian the Apostate. In conversation with others during a military feast, they condemned the emperor for his persecution of Christians. Someone told the emperor of this, and he had them thrown into prison. Some of the emperor’s men visited them with the intention of turning them away from the true Faith. They told Juventius and Maximinus that many of their companions had denied Christ. To this, the two nobly replied: “Then we must stand bravely, and offer ourselves as a sacrifice for their apostasy.” They were beheaded with the sword in the dark of night, but their relics were found and were revealed to be miracle-working.

text:
Letters from Stockholm
The President's Hand: What Fourteen Words in Green Ink Tell Us About Bola Ahmed Tinubu

By Kio Amachree

An assessment in the manner of a forensic document review. The author is not a forensic document examiner, and no law-enforcement agency has reviewed this material. Handwriting cannot prove character or schooling; what follows is an informed reading of a public document, offered as opinion and argument, and the reader is invited to look at the photograph and disagree.

1. The Exhibit

The document is a single entry in a condolence register, photographed and circulated by Intel Region. It is written in green ink on ruled paper and dated 19/09/25 in two places, once in the margin and once beneath the signature. The full text reads:

Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR. Another condolence visit to my family. May my big brother continue to rest in Aljanah Firdhaus.

Beneath it is a compressed, looping signature with a single underline. That is the entire corpus: fourteen words of prose, a name, a title, a prayer, a date. It is a very small sample, and any honest examiner would say so before saying anything else. But it is a sample written by the man himself, unscripted, in public, without a speechwriter, a teleprompter or an aide's steadying hand. In a presidency conducted almost entirely through intermediaries, that alone makes it worth reading closely.

2. Physical Description of the Writing

The hand is large. The letters occupy the full height of the ruled lines and frequently break through them, and the overall size is well above what one sees in a typical adult register entry. The strokes are heavy and continuous; there is no hesitation, no lifting of the pen mid-word to correct a form, no retracing. The writer knew what he wanted to say and put it down at speed.

The script is a mixed cursive, joined for most of a word but breaking into separated or printed forms at the capitals. The capital B in "Bola" and "Brother" is oversized and rounded, the A of "Ahmed" and "Aljanah" is a tall open loop, and the G, C, F and R of the postnominal are drawn one at a time as printed capitals rather than joined. The lower-case forms are simplified to the point of being schematic: the m and n collapse into a wave, the r is a bump, the e is often a bare hook. Legibility is moderate. A reader who did not already know the phrases would struggle with "Firdhaus" and might not recover "continue" without context.

The baseline is unsteady and drifts upward across each line. Spacing between words is generous, spacing between letters is tight. The right margin is disregarded entirely; "continue" runs to the edge of the page and the final word is pushed off the photograph. The signature is a different creature from the body text: fast, angular, mostly illegible, finished with a firm underline, and dated a second time as if the first date were not enough.

3. What a Hand Like This Suggests

I set down the following as interpretation, not finding, and I note that graphology as a science of character does not enjoy the standing its practitioners claim for it. With that said, some inferences require no mysticism at all.

The size, pressure and pace of this hand belong to a man who is accustomed to taking up space and to being read by others whether or not he makes it easy for them. There is no anxiety in it about being understood. The disregard for the margin and the second, redundant date speak to the same thing: this is a writer who does not edit himself for the reader, because he has not had to for a very long time. The oversized capitals on his own name and on "Brother" are a small vanity and a small warmth, both at once.

The fluency is real. This is not a laboured hand, and it is not the hand of someone unfamiliar with writing in English. Whoever taught him to write did so early and thoroughly enough that the motor habit has outlived everything else. The simplification of the small letters is what happens to a schooled hand after fifty years of signing rather than composing; it is the handwriting of a man who writes his name a hundred times a week and a paragraph almost never.

And the prose is correct. I will say this plainly because it cuts against a case I have made elsewhere and I owe the reader the same honesty I demand of the men I write about. "Another condolence visit to my family" is idiomatic. "May my big brother continue to rest in" is a complete and properly formed sentence. The register entry contains no grammatical error. It is short and formulaic, and a man can write a condolence formula correctly and still speak the language badly, but the formula is right.

4. The Question of Schooling

The handwriting supports the view that Bola Tinubu was schooled, in English, in his youth, and it supports nothing more precise than that. It cannot tell us where, or under what name, or for how long, and I distrust anyone who says it can.

For that we have to turn to the paper record, and the paper record is these days better known than it once was. In October 2023, under order of a United States court, Chicago State University released the records it holds on him. Those records show a student named Bola Tinubu admitted in 1977, addressed as "Mr." in the admissions letter, and graduated in 1979 with a degree in business administration. The university confirmed the attendance and the degree. It also stated that the replacement certificate he had submitted to Nigeria's electoral commission was not one it had issued, and the file contained a Southwest College record marking the student's sex as female and three different years of birth across the various documents.

I have long believed that the man in the Chicago records and the man in Aso Rock are the same person, and I believe the handwriting is consistent with that: a school-trained English hand from the correct era, degraded by decades of high office. What I do not accept, and what the record does not resolve, is the biography around those records. The dates of birth do not agree with one another. The certificate he presented to INEC is not the university's certificate. The Southwest College document is either a clerical error or something worse, and no one in authority has been willing to say which. A man who went to school under his own name and graduated honestly does not usually need three birthdays and a certificate the issuing institution disowns. The honest position is that the American schooling appears real, and the identity surrounding it remains, in places, unexplained. I put that as a question rather than a verdict because it is a question, and because his government has had three years to answer it and has preferred not to.

5. The Spoken Word Against the Written One

Here is the tension that the register entry throws into relief. The written English is competent. The spoken English, which the whole country hears every time he departs from a text, is not. He hesitates, loses the thread of a sentence, reaches for a Yoruba construction and delivers it in English words, and does so in an accent that has been untouched by the years he is said to have spent in the United States and, by some accounts, in England.

There are innocent explanations, and the fair-minded reader should hold them in view. Age is one; he was born, depending on which of his documents one believes, in 1952, 1954 or 1955, and no man's fluency improves in his seventies. Health is another, and I will not speculate about his. Written English learned in a colonial-era classroom and spoken English acquired late and used only professionally are, in any case, different competences, and it is entirely possible to command one and stumble in the other.

But the less innocent explanation is also available and a serious country would want to test it. A man who had truly lived and studied in the American Midwest for the better part of a decade, in his twenties, at the age when accents are still plastic, would be expected to carry some trace of it. He carries none. The handwriting tells us he was taught to write. It cannot tell us whether the years abroad that the official biography describes were spent as the biography describes them, and his speech gives one no confidence that they were.

6. Assessment

On the evidence of fourteen words: a confident, forceful, hurried man, long past caring whether he is easy to read, schooled early in an English hand and fluent enough on paper to write a condolence correctly. On the evidence of the record: a documented American degree wrapped in a biography that does not add up in its particulars and that its owner has never permitted to be examined. On the evidence of his mouth: a man whose spoken English does not match the life his papers describe.

None of this is a crime. It is something a democracy is entitled to know about the person it has handed its treasury and its army. The Nigerian people were asked to accept a life story on trust. A single page from a condolence register cannot confirm or refute that story. It can, and does, remind us how little of it we have ever actually been shown.

Kio Amachree writes from Stockholm and is the founder of Worldview International.

Sources consulted for the documentary record: FIJ fact-check on the CSU documents; TheCable on the CSU release; Nairametrics on the CSU release; ICIR on the CSU deposition.

text:
There Is No Heir Apparent After the Presidency: America’s “Successor’s Curse” and the 2028 Dilemma Facing Vance and Rubio

Throughout more than 240 years of American political history, a rather counterintuitive phenomenon has persisted:

The people closest to the president are often not the people most likely to become the next president.

By conventional political logic, the vice president should be the president’s most natural successor. The secretary of state, meanwhile, has traditionally been regarded as one of the cabinet officials with the strongest credentials for the presidency. Both positions are close to the center of power, provide extensive experience in national governance, and offer a level of national visibility that ordinary politicians can rarely attain.

Yet American political history tells a very different story.

If we adopt a strict definition of political succession—namely:

An incumbent vice president or secretary of state immediately succeeds the incumbent president by becoming the presidential candidate who wins the next presidential election.

—then this kind of “direct political succession” is extraordinarily rare.

There have been 50 vice presidents in American history. Fifteen of them eventually became president, but a substantial number did so not by winning a presidential election, but by assuming the presidency after the death or resignation of the incumbent. Under the stricter definition of an incumbent vice president winning the presidency in the subsequent election, only four individuals qualify: John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Martin Van Buren, and George H. W. Bush.

In other words, among the 50 vice presidents in American history, only four completed this particular form of direct political succession—roughly 8 percent.

The situation involving secretaries of state is even more striking.

The U.S. Department of State's historical records list 72 secretaries of state. Under the same strict standard, only James Madison, James Monroe, and John Quincy Adams moved directly from the secretary of state position into the presidency. All three cases occurred during the early republic, between 1809 and 1825.

Of course, figures such as Thomas Jefferson, Martin Van Buren, and James Buchanan also served as secretary of state before eventually becoming president. But they did not move directly from the secretary of state position into the presidency. Thus, if we are discussing the modern concept of a secretary of state as an immediate presidential successor, this phenomenon has virtually disappeared from American politics.

What makes these statistics important is not simply the historical coincidence.

They reveal a structural paradox in American politics:

Being closer to the presidency does not necessarily make someone more likely to become president.

A vice president or secretary of state may possess extensive experience in government, yet precisely because of that experience, he also inherits the political liabilities of the incumbent administration.

This can be described as a kind of “Successor’s Curse” in American politics.

And this curse may become particularly relevant to the Republican Party in 2028.

During Donald Trump’s second presidency, Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have both emerged as important potential figures in the Republican Party’s future presidential competition.

But their real challenge is not simply a question of “who has Trump’s favor.”

It is a much deeper question:

How can someone who has participated in governing the Trump administration convince American voters in 2028 that he is not merely an extension of the Trump administration, but a president capable of opening a new political era?

That is the structural dilemma both Vance and Rubio will face.

I. The “Successor’s Curse” in American Politics

Why is it so difficult for vice presidents and secretaries of state to complete a political succession?

The answer does not lie in any individual’s abilities. It lies in the structural tensions created by the American presidential system, the party system, and the modern electoral process.

A senior member of an incumbent administration must first demonstrate that he can faithfully execute the president’s policies. But as the presidential term draws to a close, he must suddenly convince voters that:

“I am not merely the past. I can create the future.”

This is the fundamental dilemma of the successor.

In the early American republic, genuine elite political succession did exist.

John Adams succeeded Washington. Jefferson succeeded Adams. Madison, Monroe, and John Quincy Adams subsequently formed a remarkably concentrated chain of political succession among the early republic’s governing elite.

The role of secretary of state was particularly important during this period. In the early nineteenth century, it functioned almost like a traditional pipeline for cultivating presidential candidates.

Madison, Monroe, and John Quincy Adams all moved from the secretary of state position to the White House.

But as American politics evolved from elite bargaining toward mass democracy, party primaries, television politics, and eventually social-media politics, this path gradually lost its advantage.

The reason is simple:

Modern presidential elections require far more than governing experience.

They require an entirely different set of political capabilities.

II. The First Barrier: The Double Trap of “Shadow” and “Baggage”

This is the first problem shared by both vice presidents and secretaries of state.

Whether they want it or not, senior members of an administration become associated with its successes and failures.

If the economy prospers, foreign policy succeeds, and the administration is popular, they can share in the political rewards.

But if the country experiences:

inflation;

recession;

a border crisis;
social conflict;
diplomatic failure;
war;
or a government scandal,
they cannot easily escape responsibility.
The successor is therefore trapped in a political dilemma.

If he breaks with his predecessor

He can tell voters:

“I am not the past. I represent the future.”

But the party immediately faces another question:

If you believe the policies of the past were wrong, why did you occupy such an important position within the administration?

For a vice president, this can even be interpreted as betraying the president.

For a secretary of state, it can be portrayed as political opportunism or ideological inconsistency.

If he refuses to break with his predecessor

A different problem emerges:

If you are not going to change anything, why does the country need you?

This is the successor’s “change dilemma.”

At the end of a presidential term, voters are often not simply asking:

“Who understands the current administration best?”

They are more likely to ask:

“Who can take us into the next era?”

The successor therefore inherits a great deal of the past while having to construct a political narrative about the future.

This is why vice presidents and secretaries of state are often in a more awkward position than opposition candidates.

An opposition candidate can simply say:

“The current administration has failed.”

A successor has to say:

“The current administration has been broadly right, but I can do it better.”

The latter is clearly a much more difficult political narrative.

III. The Second Barrier: Governing and Campaigning Require Different Skill Sets

This is perhaps the most important element in understanding the dilemma facing vice presidents and secretaries of state.

Governing and campaigning are not the same skill.

In some respects, they require almost opposite instincts.

An effective government official must be:

cautious;

professional;

willing to compromise;

discreet;
capable of managing complex interests;
risk-conscious;
and careful not to create unnecessary political conflict.
An effective presidential candidate, by contrast, must be able to:
simplify complex issues;
establish clear political contrasts;

build a personal brand;

generate emotional energy;
mobilize grassroots supporters;
create media moments;
and constantly command public attention.
In other words:
Governance seeks to reduce uncertainty; campaigning often seeks to create political certainty.
A governing official tends to say:

“The issue is extremely complicated and requires careful consideration.”

A campaigner must often say:

“This is the problem, and I have a clear solution.”

That is why an excellent secretary of state does not necessarily make an excellent presidential candidate.

IV. The Secretary of State’s Limitation: Foreign-Policy Capital Does Not Automatically Convert into Domestic Political Capital

The secretary of state is one of the most important executive officials in the American government.

Yet the position has a built-in problem of political-capital conversion.

The political capital accumulated by a secretary of state is concentrated primarily in foreign policy:

international crises;

alliances;

international organizations;

diplomatic negotiations;

arms control;
international trade;
war and peace;
and complex bargaining among foreign governments.
These matters are unquestionably important.
But they are not necessarily the issues that ordinary voters think about every day during a presidential election.
Unless the United States is experiencing a war, a major international crisis, or a serious national-security emergency, many swing voters are still likely to focus primarily on:
the economy, employment, the cost of living, health care, immigration, public safety, and housing.

The famous phrase from Bill Clinton’s 1992 campaign team—

“It’s the economy, stupid.”

—became a classic of American politics precisely because presidential elections have a very practical dimension:

Foreign-policy achievements often operate at the level of grand strategy, while votes are frequently determined by household economics.

This creates a political-capital mismatch for secretaries of state.

A secretary of state may be extremely skilled at answering questions such as:

How should the United States deal with China?

How should it deal with Russia?

How should it maintain its European alliances?

How should it manage the Middle East?

But voters may ask something very different:

Why is my rent so expensive?

Why have food prices gone up?

Why can't my children find good jobs?

What are you actually going to do about the border?

If a secretary of state cannot demonstrate meaningful governing competence on these domestic questions, his foreign-policy record may not automatically translate into presidential-election credibility.

There is an additional danger:

Diplomatic skill itself can become a political liability.

The essence of diplomacy is often compromise, exchange, and balancing competing interests.

But during a domestic election campaign, an opponent can easily repackage diplomatic compromise as:

“Giving in to foreign governments.”

“Sacrificing American interests.”

“Weakness.”

“Globalism.”

Thus, the more accustomed a secretary of state is to compromise in international affairs, the more he may have to explain during a presidential campaign:

Why is diplomatic compromise not weakness, but a means of advancing American interests?

This is a classic case of political-capital conversion loss.

V. The Vice President’s Limitation: He Must Demonstrate Leadership Without Acting Like the President

The vice president faces an even more unusual dilemma.

The vice president is not a completely independent political actor.

First and foremost, he must demonstrate:

Loyalty to the president.

The president can develop an independent policy brand, but the vice president cannot easily construct a political platform that openly contradicts the president.

Otherwise, he risks being perceived as:

attempting to seize power;

excessively ambitious;

disloyal to the president;

or creating a competing center of power within the administration.

Yet as the presidential term draws to an end, the vice president must suddenly tell voters:

“Now you should choose me.”
This creates a strange identity paradox:
In government, he must prove that he is not the president;
on the campaign trail, he must prove that he is capable of becoming president.
This is the vice president’s political dilemma.

He cannot completely distance himself from the president, but neither can he remain permanently in the president’s shadow.

He must navigate an extraordinarily narrow path between loyalty and independence.

VI. The Third Barrier: “Change Fatigue” and the Voter’s Periodic Desire for a New Direction

The candidates’ structural problems are compounded by another feature of American electoral psychology.
After four years of presidential rule, virtually every problem associated with the government eventually becomes associated with the governing party.

Whether or not the president personally caused the problem, voters can develop a simple instinct:

“You have been in power long enough. Let’s try someone else.”

Of course, American history does not contain a mechanical rule of automatic four-year partisan rotation.

The real issue is this:

An incumbent party must continually convince voters that continuing under the same political leadership is still necessary.

A successor therefore has to accomplish two contradictory tasks:

Enjoy the governing party’s record of achievement.

while simultaneously:

Escaping the governing party’s political liabilities.

That is much harder than what an opposition candidate has to do.

VII. The Fourth Barrier: The Modern Primary System Continuously Creates Incentives for Anti-Establishment Candidates

America’s modern presidential nomination system has also weakened traditional forms of political succession.

As presidential nominations have increasingly depended on state-level primaries and grassroots voters, political seniority itself has ceased to guarantee the nomination.

A vice president, secretary of state, senator, or cabinet official may possess an exceptionally strong résumé, but he must still return to the grassroots and face voters.

And there is an important difference between a party primary and a general election:

A primary is not necessarily about choosing the candidate most acceptable to all Americans. It is about choosing the candidate most capable of inspiring the party’s own voters.

This creates enormous opportunities for outsiders and dark-horse candidates.

A governor can say:

“I am not part of Washington.”

A business executive can say:

“I have never been a political bureaucrat.”

A political newcomer can say:

“They have been running the country for decades. Now it is our turn.”

A vice president or secretary of state has difficulty using such language.

Because they cannot deny the obvious:

They are part of the government.

VIII. The Fifth Barrier: Governors Possess an “Independent Governing Record” That Vice Presidents and Secretaries of State Often Lack

Modern American presidential candidates who are governors often possess a particular advantage. It is not simply that they appear more “in touch with ordinary people.”

More importantly:

A governor has an independent executive record.

A governor can tell voters:

I have governed a state.

I have managed a budget.

I have reformed education.

I have handled natural disasters.

I have improved employment.

Whatever one thinks of those accomplishments, they belong to the candidate personally.

The vice president faces a fundamental problem:

His record is difficult to separate from the president’s.

For the secretary of state, the problem is even clearer:

His record is concentrated primarily in foreign affairs.

A governor can therefore present himself as:

“Someone who has already proven that he can govern.”

Vice presidents and secretaries of state often have to spend much more time proving:

“Although I have not independently led the national government, I nevertheless possess the ability to lead it.”

This is an independent governing-record deficit.

IX. Vance’s Dilemma: He Must Answer the Question, “What Is Vanceism After Trump?”

By 2028, J.D. Vance’s challenge will involve far more than competition within the Republican Party.

His real question will be:

Does Trumpism belong to Donald Trump personally, or has it become part of the Republican Party itself?

This is both Vance’s greatest opportunity and his greatest risk.

His greatest political advantage is that he does not have the same historical distance from Trumpism that Rubio does.

He is young, and he has demonstrated an ability to translate the political language of the Trump era into a form that can resonate with a younger generation of Republicans.

If Trumpism becomes institutionalized, Vance could possess an enormous advantage:

He could become the most natural political successor to Trump.

But there is a trap.

He cannot simply become a copy of Trump.

Trump possesses an extraordinarily distinctive personal political brand:

a celebrity-like persona;

a unique command of media attention;

a powerful personal brand;

decades of accumulated political identity;

and an unusually strong personal loyalty among segments of the electorate.

These assets cannot simply be inherited.

Vance therefore faces a classic “shadow dilemma.”

If he is too much like Trump

Voters may ask:

“Why not simply continue with Trumpism itself?”

If he is too different from Trump
Republican grassroots voters may ask:
“If you are so different from Trump, why are you the heir to Trumpism?”
Therefore, what Vance ultimately needs to build is not:
Trump 2.0.

but:

a new Republican version for the post-Trump era.

That will be his central political task.

X. Rubio’s Dilemma: He Must Prove That He Is Not the “Last Representative of the Old Republican Party”

Rubio’s problem is almost the opposite of Vance’s.

He has greater political experience and an extensive background in Congress and foreign affairs.

But that experience is itself a double-edged sword.

Rubio must answer a fundamental question:

Does he represent the Republican Party after Trump, or the Republican Party before Trump?

If the Republican Party in 2028 continues to emphasize America First, anti-globalism, immigration restriction, and skepticism toward the traditional foreign-policy establishment, Rubio will have to demonstrate:

that he has genuinely completed his political transformation.

In other words, he must convince Republican grassroots voters:

“I am not the Marco Rubio of the old Republican Party.”

But if he moves too far toward Trumpism, he risks losing his own independent political identity.

Rubio therefore faces his own version of the “shadow problem.”

His shadow is not Donald Trump himself.

It is:

the traditional Republican establishment.

His real challenge is to complete a political transformation:

from a traditional Republican foreign-policy figure into a post-Trump Republican national strategist.

If he succeeds, his experience will become a major asset.

If he fails, that same experience may become evidence that he belongs to an older political era.

XI. Vance and Rubio Represent Two Very Different Models of Succession

Vance and Rubio can therefore be understood as representing two different models of political succession.

Vance represents “internal succession.”

His logic is:

Trump transformed the Republican Party. I will carry that transformation forward.

His advantage is:

A relatively close ideological relationship with the Republican grassroots.

His risk is:

How to escape Trump’s enormous personal shadow.

Rubio represents something closer to “integrative succession.”

His logic might be:

Trump transformed the Republican Party, but I can combine this new Republicanism with the institutional experience of the traditional Republican Party.

His advantages are:

experience, foreign-policy expertise, and broad policy knowledge.

His risk is:

whether he can convince the Republican grassroots of the Trump era that he has genuinely completed his political transformation.

The competition between them is therefore not merely a competition between two individuals.

It may represent a larger choice between two possible futures for the Republican Party:

the continuation and institutionalization of Trumpism

versus

a renewed synthesis between Trumpism and traditional Republicanism.

XII. The Real Question: Will America Still Want a “Successor” in 2028?

Ultimately, Vance and Rubio’s greatest common opponent may not be each other.

It may be a much more fundamental question:

Will American voters in 2028 still want to live on the political trajectory of the Trump era?

If the American economy is performing well in 2028, if the Trump administration has accumulated a clear record of governing achievements, and if Republican voters believe that Trump has completed a historic transformation of the party, voters may want:

“Continue Trumpism, but with someone younger and more institutional.”

Under those circumstances, Vance could have a major advantage.

But if Trumpism has generated significant political fatigue by 2028, or Republican voters begin to conclude:

“The Trump era has accomplished what it needed to accomplish.”

then a new governor, a younger outsider, or a candidate capable of rebuilding a coalition between traditional Republicanism and Trumpism could rise rapidly.

At that point, Vance’s question will change from:

“How do I succeed Trump?”

to:

“How do I move beyond Trump?”

And Rubio’s question will change from:

“How do I prove that I have embraced Trumpism?”

to:

“How do I prove that I can represent the Republican Party after Trump?”

These questions may sound similar, but they are fundamentally different.

Conclusion: What Is Hardest for an American President to Pass On Is Not Power, but the Future

The so-called “Successor’s Curse” in American political history is not a mysterious historical fate.

It is better understood as a structural outcome.

Vice presidents and secretaries of state are closest to the center of power, so they have the greatest opportunity to inherit executive experience. But precisely because they are so close to the center of power, they are also the most likely to inherit the political liabilities of the incumbent administration.

In government, what they need is:

governing ability.

On the presidential campaign trail, however, what they need is:

the ability to embody change, a personal brand, mass-mobilization skills, and a compelling vision of the future.

They face an almost irresolvable paradox:

If they embrace the past, they lack the sense of change voters may desire; if they reject the past, they must explain why they were part of that past in the first place.

The vice president’s dilemma is:

He cannot betray the president, yet he must ultimately prove that he is not the president’s shadow.

The secretary of state’s dilemma is:

He may possess substantial political capital in foreign affairs, yet he must convert that capital into credibility on domestic governance.

Meanwhile, America’s modern primary system continues to create opportunities for political newcomers who carry fewer Washington liabilities and can more easily embody a sense of “change.”

Therefore, the real question facing Vance and Rubio in 2028 is not simply:

“Who can succeed Trump?”

It is a much deeper political question:

After Trump, does the Republican Party need a successor—or does it need an innovator?

If American voters want a successor, Vance may possess a natural advantage. If they want an innovator, anyone too heavily dependent on Trump’s political legacy could find himself at a disadvantage.

That is the brutal reality of American presidential politics:

A politician must first prove that he can inherit the past—and then prove that he can transcend it.

And presidential elections ultimately tend to reward not the person closest to the center of power, but the person who can most convincingly make voters believe:

“The next page will be written by me.”

text:
This would be the upset of the day, but Trading Assistant is taking it.

Dodgers vs Nationals…

Here’s the read:

The Read: I lean toward the Washington Nationals (ML +228).

The Fundamentals:
This matchup features an enormous starting pitching advantage for Los Angeles, but a massive situational catalyst completely changes the math. The Dodgers are sending Blake Snell, who is pitching at an elite level (2.42 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, .170 opponent average). Washington counters with Jackson Kent, who is bleeding traffic with a 1.71 WHIP. 

Normally, this pitching gap—especially with the wind blowing out to center field at 7 mph—would make the Dodgers an overwhelming favorite against a pitcher who allows that much contact. However, the Dodgers are without both Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman tonight. Removing two MVP-caliber bats from the top of the lineup drastically lowers Los Angeles's offensive ceiling and run-scoring potential, making them heavily reliant on Snell to pitch a flawless game. 

While the Dodgers are still the better team, a 70%+ implied probability for a lineup missing its two best hitters is simply too high. I make the Nationals' true win probability closer to 36%.

Market Pricing & Execution:
The sportsbook has the Dodgers priced as massive home favorites at -285, leaving the Nationals at +228 (29.2% fair value). Polymarket currently has the Nationals to win priced at 30¢. (I wasn't able to isolate this specific game on Kalshi, though I see from your portfolio history that you frequently trade Dodgers and Nationals markets there).

With my read at 36% for Washington, there is a playable ~6.8-point edge on the underdog. My calibration data shows that trusting these larger (5+ point) edge calculations when we disagree with the market has been our most actionable and profitable strategy (16-4 on resolved calls). The market is pricing the Dodgers as if their lineup is fully intact, completely undervaluing the impact of missing Ohtani and Freeman.

For execution, Polymarket offers a slightly better number. The sportsbook's +228 moneyline carries a raw break-even of ~30.5%, while Polymarket offers the Nationals at 30¢ (30% break-even). The best execution is taking Nationals YES at 30¢ on Polymarket.

text:
Lean Hog Futures Weekly Outlook - August 31–September 4, 2026

Top News Story: October Hogs Slip on Friday Profit Taking as Market Prepares for Post Labor Day Fundamentals

The lean hog complex ended the first week of September on a softer note, giving back mid week gains on Friday as traders squared positions ahead of the extended Labor Day holiday weekend. 

Following a strong mid-week push that carried benchmark October futures back into the $83.00–$84.00 range, Friday’s pre holiday session saw active contracts pull back.

The primary driver behind the market’s underlying firmness earlier in the week was a steadying cash index and stable export pace, though packers continue to exercise strict procurement discipline. 

While negotiated spot cash bids were quiet into Friday morning, wholesale carcass cutout values managed to hold near the $91.00 level, keeping overall packer margins relatively workable.

With US markets closed on Monday for Labor Day, traders are looking ahead to next week’s post holiday session to evaluate whether fall slaughter expansion will keep cash prices under pressure or if retail pipeline replenishment provides fresh support.

Market Notes
The CME Lean Hog Index showed moderate stability heading into September, ticking up 23 cents on Wednesday to settle at $91.08. Negotiated cash trade saw thin volume to close out Friday morning, keeping the index closely watched as a benchmark for October paper.

The wholesale cutout experienced light mid-week volatility before steadying. The USDA Friday morning pork carcass cutout value was reported up 14 cents at $91.26 per cwt, with most primal cuts holding solid ground except for hams.

Federally inspected slaughter for Thursday was estimated at 467,000 head, bringing the week to date total to 1.883 million head down 18,000 head from the previous week as plants adjusted processing schedules ahead of the long weekend.

Price Summary and Recent Movements
Futures prices faced pre holiday profit taking on Friday, trimming weekly advances but keeping intermediate support levels intact. Performance metrics at the close of Friday, September 4, 2026:

October 2026 (HEV26): 82.400, down 1.050 (Daily), pulling back from mid-week highs above 84.00.

December 2026 (HEZ26): 72.450, down 1.475 (Daily), settling near lower fall ranges.

February 2027 (HEG27): 75.100, down 1.500 (Daily), consolidating within winter cyclical frames.

April 2027 (HEJ27): 78.425, down 1.200 (Daily), tracking long-term seasonal spreads.

Cash Trade: Friday morning CME Lean Hog Index at $91.08; Friday morning pork carcass cutout value at $91.26.

Key Market Factors

Supply: Daily slaughter runs near 467,000 head signal consistent marketings, though total weekly slaughter fell to 1.883 million head due to pre holiday plant adjustments.

Demand: Export activity continues to offer reliable support, with recent USDA Weekly Export Sales figures showing solid sales of 34,978 MT of pork for 2026, driven by top buyers including Mexico.

External: Broad livestock complex volatility and ongoing economic scrutiny keep managed capital conservative, though firmness in feeder cattle and steady export movement offer underlying support.

Technicals: October hogs met resistance near the $84.00 level during mid week trading before retreating on Friday. Major support remains established near the late-August low of $79.675.

Upcoming USDA Reports Expectations
When trading resumes on Tuesday following Labor Day, market attention will shift to post holiday procurement strategies. 

Traders will closely monitor whether packers raise cash bids to fill processing schedules after Monday's plant closures. 

Weekly export tracking and the weekly USDA Hogs & Pigs/Cold Storage data updates later in September will also be evaluated for supply confirmation.

Funds Activity
Managed money positioning remained relatively stable over the holiday-shortened frame. While commodity trading advisors trimmed long exposure during Friday's pullback, overall short side pressure was limited, indicating that institutional funds prefer a neutral stance until clear fundamental trends emerge post Labor Day.

Outlook for the Week Ahead
The near-term trajectory leans neutral to rangebound. With the CME index near $91.00 and October futures holding above $82.00, the contract remains within a defined consolidation pattern. 

The market will look for post holiday packer demand to determine whether October paper can mount another test of overhead resistance or resume cash convergence.

Risks: A breakdown below the $80.00 psychological support floor, or post-holiday weakness in primal cutout values.

Strategy: Neutral to cautious. Keep tight risk management on long positions until October futures convincingly break above intermediate technical resistance levels.

Weaponization report: Richmond FBI 'revolt' followed rebuke over Catholic memo | Rowan Scarborough, The Washington Times

July 2023 was a soul-searching month for the FBI’s field office in Richmond, Virginia. The office’s analysts didn’t like the way the Washington headquarters treated them and would eventually need therapeutic counseling, a new Justice Department report says.

Earlier that year, the field office produced a confidential intelligence product now known as the “Richmond Catholic Memo.” It linked the area’s nontraditional, 49-year-old Our Lady of Fatima Chapel with a global network of anti-Vatican priests, the Society of St. PiusX (SSPX).

The memo suggested the alliance presented an extremist threat here at home. The field office even assigned operators to surveil two priests.

All of this was done in secret until Kyle Seraphin, an ex-agent and whistleblower, posted the memo that February.

Catholic leaders found the allegations offensive. So did FBI headquarters, then under the supervision of FBI Director Christopher Wray.

The memo read more like a description of Antifa than traditional Latin-loving Catholics.

Second-term President Trump ordered the creation of a Justice Department “Weaponization Working Group” to investigate alleged abuse of power during the Biden years. The Richmond memo fit the bill. The department on Aug. 28 released over 200 pages of narrative and exhibits.

The report said the FBI Inspection Division concluded in 2023 that the memo’s creators lacked “professional judgment and failed to adhere to FBI standards.” All involved should be “admonished.”

How did the field office take the criticism? Not well. Agents staged a mini-revolt, the DOJ report tells us.

“The Richmond Field Office did not agree with the criticisms of the internal review. On July 7, 2023, the Special Agent in Charge held a staff meeting at the Richmond Field Office to preview the Inspection Division’s findings. Notes from that meeting reveal that many in the office, including the Special Agent in Charge, disagreed with the Inspection Division’s report.”

According to the notes, the assistant special agent in charge said, “There are no inconsistent performers in this room.” And his boss, the agent in charge, “apologized” to his staff for Washington’s rebuke.

The report also said, “When Intelligence Analyst 2 said in an e-mail that she was ’terribly sorry for all that everyone has had to endure as a result of this product,’ the Special Agent in Charge told her she need not apologize, saying that the event ’will make for a great chapter in your memoirs some day!’”

The revolt was not done. Three weeks later, at an all-employee meeting, the report said, “Leadership at the Richmond Field Office expressed … ’that people involved didn’t deserve this.’” Supervisors offered “Employee Assistance Counselors.”

Here is how the FBI field office wrote the first paragraph of the Richmond Catholic Memo, as circulated internally on Jan. 23, 2023.

“FBI Richmond assesses the increasingly observed interest of racially or ethnically motivated violent extremists (RMVEs) in radical-traditionalist Catholic (RTC) ideology almost certainly presents opportunities for threat mitigation through the exploration of new avenues for tripwire and source development. FBI Richmond makes this assessment with high confidence based on FBI investigations, local law enforcement agency reporting and liaison reporting, with varying degrees of corroboration and access.”

Here’s why the Richmond office should never have written the report.

It largely revolved around one bad actor, a right-wing criminal who made plans to blow up targets and has been sent to prison twice. He considered himself a radical Catholic. He made a brief attempted connection to the Lady of Fatima Chapel, taking a catechism course. But as the priest explained to the FBI, he was never allowed to join or go to confession.

The Richmond field office only identified two other supposed radicals, one in Portland, Oregon, who had died, and the second in Milwaukee.

That was about it.

Another problem. Richmond showed its liberal bias. FBI analysts relied on the disgraced Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) for how to define dangerous Catholics. The field office ignored the fact that the SPLC is staffed by conservative haters who like to attach the “hate” label to people with whom it disagrees.

It was the SPLC years ago that coined a new label, “Radical Traditionalist Catholics (RTC),” which the Richmond field office readily adopted in the lead memo paragraph.

The two news media cited in the Richmond Memo — what the FBI calls “Open Source” — were the ultraliberal The Atlantic and Salon.

And then there is the memo’s language.

A slide presentation on how to recognize “Radical Traditionalist Catholics” (RTC) lists “conservative family values/roles,” the “rejection of modernity” and “tendency toward isolationism.”

The Trump Justice report says, “The Memo did not provide concrete examples of the differences between ’radical-traditionalist Catholics’ and traditionalist Catholics, indicating that the key metric was simply how traditionalist a particular Catholic group was.”

The field office also mapped out a network of other Catholic institutions in the Richmond area for whom parishioners could serve as informants.

The Richmond Catholic Memo listed names, addresses and phone numbers and said the FBI should engage each institution’s leadership to “sensitize [the] congregations to the warning signs of radicalization and enlist their assistance to serve as suspicious activity tripwires.”

But Mr. Seraphin’s publication of the memo ended Richmond’s grand plan.

Washington headquarters ordered the memo deleted from the FBI database.

And today.

“The FBI personnel involved in the creation of the Richmond Catholic Memo have been terminated from their positions,” said the Weaponization Working Group.
