text:
A Rhino Just Destroyed a Watermelon With Its Face. Here's the Actual Science of How — and Why a Zoo Wanted Him To.

The clip is simple enough to describe in one sentence: a black rhinoceros at the Oregon Zoo leans down low, presses the sharp tip of its horn into a whole ripe watermelon sitting a few short inches from a ground-level camera, and splits it wide open like the fruit had never once stood a chance. Juice everywhere. Rind cracking clean along one neat almost surgical line. Then that huge, strangely delicate, prehensile upper lip goes to work scooping out the red interior while the ground-level camera captures every wrinkle on a face built like continental crust.

It's a satisfying, oddly cathartic sixteen seconds of destruction. It's also a genuinely interesting piece of biology hiding behind a fun video, because almost nothing about what you just watched works the way most people assume — starting with the weapon doing all that damage.

THE HORN ISN'T BONE. IT ISN'T EVEN ATTACHED TO ANYTHING.

Here's the fact that surprises almost everyone the first time they hear it: a rhino horn contains no bone core at all. Unlike deer antlers or the horns of cattle and sheep, which grow from a bony core anchored to the skull, a rhinoceros horn is made entirely of keratin — the exact same structural protein that makes up human hair and fingernails, and the outer layer of horse hooves. It grows directly up from the skin on the snout, in tightly compacted, fibrous layers, sitting on a roughened patch of skull bone without being fused to it the way antlers are, which is part of why a rhino can survive losing a horn entirely to injury or trimming, in a way no deer could ever survive losing an antler mid-growth.

That single fact rewrites almost everything about how you should picture the watermelon-cracking moment. This isn't a rhino swinging a bony spike built into its skeleton. It's a rhino pressing a dense, tightly packed mass of compressed hair-protein — solid enough, layered enough, and hard enough at the tip to functionally behave like a blunt weapon, but biologically closer in composition to a very large, very aggressively shaped fingernail than to a bone or tusk. Researchers who've studied horn structure under magnification describe it as something like a bundle of keratin filaments cemented together with a calcium and melanin-rich matrix, a bit like a fistful of pencils glued into a single wedge — strong along its length, but also, notably, capable of regrowing if damaged or even, in managed conservation settings, safely trimmed back without harming the animal, the same basic way a fingernail or hoof can be trimmed.

THE LIP DOING THE ACTUAL EATING IS THE REAL STAR

Watch the clip again, past the crack of the rind, and the more remarkable tool on display isn't the horn at all — it's the mouth going in afterward. Black rhinos, specifically, have a distinctive hooked, pointed upper lip, flexible and genuinely prehensile, meaning it can curl, grip, and manipulate food with real dexterity, closer in function to an elephant's trunk-tip or a giraffe's tongue than to the flat, wide muzzle of a grazing animal like a cow or horse.

That's not a random anatomical quirk. It's a direct signature of diet. Black rhinos are browsers, not grazers — meaning their natural feeding strategy in the wild revolves around selectively plucking leaves, twigs, and shoots from bushes and low trees, rather than the wide, sweeping bites a grass-eating white rhino takes with its comparatively flat, broad lip. (White rhinos, confusingly, aren't white at all — the name is widely believed to be a mistranslation of the Afrikaans "wyd," meaning wide, referring to that flat grazing lip, and black rhinos got their name mainly as a leftover contrast rather than an accurate color description, since both species are actually a similar shade of grey.) A hooked, mobile lip built for picking individual leaves off a thorny branch turns out to be exactly the right tool for hooking into a cracked-open watermelon and scooping the sweet interior out in efficient, targeted bites — the same precise grasping motion, just redirected at a much easier target than a thorn bush.

WHY A ZOO IS HANDING A RHINO A WHOLE WATERMELON IN THE FIRST PLACE

This is where the clip stops being just a fun destruction video and becomes something with real conservation science underneath it. Zoos accredited by major accrediting bodies are required to provide what's called environmental enrichment — deliberate, structured activities and objects designed to encourage an animal's natural behaviors, engage its senses, and prevent the boredom and repetitive stress behaviors that can develop in captive animals without enough mental stimulation. A whole, unprocessed piece of produce, placed at ground level rather than simply dropped into a food trough, is a textbook enrichment technique: it forces the animal to problem-solve, to use natural tools like a horn or a trunk or claws to access the food, and to spend meaningfully more time and effort obtaining a meal than it would need to for the same calories served pre-cut in a bowl.

For a rhino specifically, a whole watermelon serves double duty. Nutritionally, it's a treat rather than a dietary staple — rhinos in professional care are generally fed a carefully balanced diet of hay, browse, and specially formulated pellets, with fruit used sparingly, in controlled portions, as a training or enrichment reward rather than a primary food source, partly because fruit's natural sugar content is much higher than anything in a rhino's typical wild diet. Behaviorally, though, cracking open a tough-skinned object to reach food inside is a genuinely close analog to real foraging challenges browsing rhinos face in the wild — thick-barked branches, thorny acacia, tough-skinned wild fruit — giving a zoo-housed rhino a chance to exercise the exact horn-and-lip coordination its body evolved to use daily, even though the specific object in front of it happens to be a supermarket watermelon instead of a wild shrub.

THE CAMERA ANGLE ISN'T AN ACCIDENT EITHER

There's a reason this footage looks the way it does — shot from ground level, inches from the action, close enough to see individual wrinkles on a face most visitors would normally view from a safe distance across an enclosure. Placing a durable, low-mounted action camera directly at an enrichment station has become an increasingly common technique at modern zoos specifically because it does two jobs at once: it gives keepers and researchers a genuinely useful, close-up record of natural feeding behavior for study and welfare monitoring, and it produces exactly the kind of visceral, up-close social media content that's become one of modern zoos' most effective public engagement and conservation-messaging tools. A shaky, distant phone video of a rhino eating fruit across an enclosure gets a few polite views. A crisp, ground-level, inches-from-the-crunch shot of the same behavior routinely finds an audience in the millions — and that audience, whether they realize it while watching, is absorbing a small, genuine piece of rhino biology and conservation messaging along with the entertainment.

THE PART OF THIS STORY THAT ISN'T FUN AT ALL

It would be a disservice to a clip this charming to leave out the harder context sitting directly underneath it, because the same horn cracking a watermelon for laughs is also the single reason black rhinos are critically endangered in the wild today. Rhino horn has long been targeted by poachers for use in traditional medicine markets, primarily across parts of Asia, despite it being made of keratin — the same material as your own fingernails — with no verified pharmacological effect beyond what any keratin supplement would provide, a point conservation scientists and medical researchers have made repeatedly and publicly for decades. It's also increasingly sought as a status symbol and, more recently, has been carved into ornamental items and jewelry in some markets, adding an entirely separate demand pressure with no dietary or medicinal justification at all.

The black rhino population collapsed catastrophically across the twentieth century, falling by an estimated 96 percent between roughly 1970 and the early 1990s due to intensive poaching, before conservation programs, anti-poaching enforcement, and protected habitat management began stabilizing and slowly rebuilding numbers in specific, closely managed populations across parts of Africa. The species remains classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the global authority on extinction risk, with total wild numbers still only a small fraction of historic populations despite the recovery. Every rhino living in an accredited zoo today, cracking watermelons for an audience of millions, exists at least partly as an ambassador for that exact crisis — a healthy, safe, closely studied representative of a species still fighting to recover from a horn trade with, ironically, no legitimate purpose behind it whatsoever.

WHAT THE ZOO SETTING ACTUALLY PROTECTS

That context reframes what looks, at first glance, like pure viral fun into something with real institutional purpose behind it. Accredited zoos participating in coordinated species survival programs maintain detailed genetic and breeding records across their captive rhino populations specifically to preserve genetic diversity as a hedge against the kind of population bottleneck black rhinos have already suffered once in living memory. Every individual animal, including the one demolishing a watermelon in this clip, represents a data point and a genetic asset in that broader, decades-long conservation effort — alongside field-based anti-poaching work, habitat protection, and community-partnership conservation programs operating directly in the rhino's native range, which most accredited zoos help fund, directly or indirectly, through a portion of admission revenue and dedicated conservation grants.

None of that makes the watermelon any less funny to watch get demolished, and it shouldn't. Good conservation communication has never required grim delivery — a joyful, visceral, honestly hilarious sixteen seconds of a rhino using genuinely fascinating anatomy to solve a genuinely real problem (how do I get to the food inside this thing) does more real-world work for public engagement with an endangered species than a somber documentary segment most people would scroll straight past. The horn cracking the rind is real biology. The lip curling around the red flesh is real biology. And the reason millions of strangers are watching a rhino do either of those things at all, rather than reading about the species in a textbook, is a species-survival story still very much in progress.

WHAT SPECIES OF RHINO ARE WE ACTUALLY LOOKING AT

Worth pausing to be precise about identification, since "rhino" covers five living species with meaningfully different builds, ranges, and conservation stories. There are two African species — the black rhino and the white rhino — and three Asian species: the greater one-horned (or Indian) rhino, the Sumatran rhino, and the Javan rhino, the latter two among the rarest large mammals on Earth, with wild populations numbering in the dozens for Sumatran rhinos and barely more than a handful of isolated populations for Javan rhinos. The animal in this clip, based on the hooked, pointed upper lip and the horn shape and posture, reads clearly as a black rhino, the species this article has focused on throughout — but it's worth knowing the wider family tree exists, because "rhino" as a single mental category badly undersells just how different these five species actually are from one another in diet, behavior, social structure, and, critically, how close each one currently sits to extinction.

The Sumatran rhino in particular deserves a mention any time rhino conservation comes up, because it's arguably in a more acute crisis than the black rhino discussed above — a smaller, hairier, more solitary forest species now reduced to a scattering of individuals across fragmented habitat in Indonesia, with conservationists increasingly relying on intensive, hands-on breeding programs simply to keep the species viable at all. Against that backdrop, a black rhino thriving in a modern zoo, healthy enough to demolish a watermelon with gusto for a camera, represents a comparatively good-news chapter in a family of species whose overall conservation picture ranges from cautiously recovering to genuinely dire.

HOW A HORN ACTUALLY GROWS BACK, AND WHY THAT MATTERS FOR CONSERVATION

The keratin composition discussed earlier isn't just a fun biology fact — it's become a genuinely important conservation tool. Because rhino horn is structurally similar to a fingernail or a hoof, it can, under veterinary supervision, be safely trimmed down close to the skin without causing the animal pain or lasting harm, in much the same way a farrier trims a horse's hoof or a groomer trims an overgrown claw. Wildlife conservation programs in parts of Africa have used exactly this technique — proactive, humane dehorning of live rhinos — as an anti-poaching strategy, on the straightforward logic that a rhino with little to no horn remaining is a dramatically less appealing target for poachers seeking horn to sell, even though it does nothing to address demand directly and remains a debated, imperfect tool rather than a complete solution on its own.

The horn does regrow, gradually, over a period of years, following roughly the same growth pattern as a fingernail growing back after a trim, though considerably slower given its far greater size and density — full regrowth to original length can take several years depending on the individual animal and how much material was removed. That regrowth capacity is precisely why dehorning programs require repeated intervention over an animal's lifetime rather than a single one-time procedure, and why researchers monitoring dehorned rhino populations track regrowth rates closely, both for animal welfare reasons and to plan the timing of future safe trims.

A CLOSER LOOK AT THAT REMARKABLE LIP

It's worth spending a little more time on the anatomical feature that arguably does more of the actual eating in this clip than the horn does. A black rhino's prehensile upper lip isn't just hooked in shape — it's genuinely muscular and mobile, capable of wrapping around a small branch or twig and stripping leaves off with real precision, the same basic biomechanical trick elephants perform with the tip of their trunk, just achieved through completely different anatomy arriving at a similar functional solution through convergent evolution. Researchers who study browsing herbivore feeding mechanics note that this kind of specialized, mobile lip or muzzle structure tends to show up repeatedly, independently, across very different mammal lineages that share one thing in common: a diet built around selectively picking specific plant parts off woody vegetation rather than sweeping up large volumes of ground-level grass, where a flatter, wider mouth works better.

Watching that same lip curl into a cracked-open watermelon and methodically scoop out the sweet red flesh is, in a real sense, watching a tool evolved for thornbush foraging get repurposed, cleanly and efficiently, for what amounts to a much easier version of the same basic task. The rhino isn't improvising a new skill for the watermelon. It's applying a well-practiced one to an unusually cooperative target, and doing so with a level of fine motor control that's easy to underestimate simply because the animal wielding it weighs somewhere in the neighborhood of a small car.

WHY WATERMELON SPECIFICALLY, AND NOT SOME OTHER FRUIT

Zoo nutritionists and keepers who design enrichment programs don't pick produce at random, and watermelon shows up disproportionately often in exactly this kind of enrichment content for a few practical reasons worth naming. Its thick, tough rind provides genuine resistance, forcing an animal to actually work at breaching it rather than getting an easy, instant reward — exactly the kind of effort-to-payoff ratio enrichment specialists look for when designing a task meant to occupy an animal's attention and problem-solving faculties for a meaningful stretch of time rather than seconds. Its high water content also makes it a useful, appealing way to encourage hydration in warm weather, particularly for large animals that can benefit from extra fluid intake during hot summer months. And its size — large enough to require real, sustained effort from an animal the size of a rhino, rather than being demolished in a single bite the way a smaller fruit would be — scales appropriately to a multi-hundred-kilogram animal in a way a single apple or orange simply wouldn't.

Zoos have used the exact same basic technique, adapted to scale and dexterity, across a huge range of species: primates working to extract food from puzzle feeders, big cats working to breach frozen "blood-cicles" packed with meat, elephants working to extract treats from suspended, weighted enrichment devices. The watermelon-and-rhino-horn pairing in this clip is a specific, well-suited instance of a much broader, deliberately engineered category of zoo animal care, not an improvised one-off.

THE BROADER TREND OF ZOOS GOING VIRAL WITH SCIENCE ATTACHED

This clip also belongs to a genuinely interesting, fairly recent shift in how zoos communicate with the public. For much of the twentieth century, zoo outreach ran mainly through school field trips, on-site signage, and occasional television documentary segments — slow-moving, low-reach channels compared to what's available today. Modern accredited zoos increasingly run dedicated social media operations specifically designed to pair short, highly shareable animal footage with genuine educational and conservation content in the caption or accompanying material, precisely because that combination reaches vastly larger, younger, more geographically dispersed audiences than traditional zoo outreach ever could on its own.

The strategy works because it doesn't ask the audience to choose between entertainment and education — it delivers both in the same sixteen seconds, letting the visceral, funny, satisfying destruction of a watermelon serve as the hook that gets someone to actually read the caption explaining what a rhino's horn is made of, why the species is endangered, or what the zoo is doing to help. It's a markedly more effective version of exactly the same educational mission zoos have always claimed to serve, just delivered through a format built for an audience that scrolls rather than one that sits through a lecture.

ONE MORE THING WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU SCROLL PAST

If there's a single fact from all of this worth repeating to someone else the next time this clip or one like it comes up, let it be this: nothing about rhino horn justifies the trade that's driven the species toward extinction. It isn't bone, it isn't magic, and decades of chemical analysis have found no properties in it beyond what any comparable mass of compacted keratin would offer — which is to say, essentially none of the medicinal effects long attributed to it in the markets still driving demand. Every fact in this piece, from the hooked lip to the enrichment watermelon to the horn's actual composition, exists in service of one underlying point: this is a genuinely remarkable animal, doing something genuinely remarkable with genuinely fascinating anatomy, and the greatest threat it faces has nothing to do with biology and everything to do with a persistent, correctable human misunderstanding about what, exactly, that horn actually is.

THE SPEED OF THAT CRACK IS ITS OWN LITTLE PHYSICS LESSON

There's one more detail worth appreciating purely as physics: the specific, clean way the rind splits. A watermelon rind is a layered structure — a thin, waxy outer skin over a thicker, spongy white layer — built by the plant to resist exactly the kind of blunt impact a fall from a vine or a peck from a bird might deliver, but not remotely built to withstand a concentrated point of pressure from something as narrow and hard as a rhino horn tip. Applying force through a small contact area, rather than a broad, flat one, dramatically increases the effective pressure at that point for the same total force, which is the same basic principle behind why a knife cuts and a hammer merely dents, and why the rhino's horn, despite moving comparatively slowly and deliberately in this clip rather than swinging with real velocity, is still more than capable of popping the rind cleanly along a stress line rather than simply bruising it. It's less a demonstration of raw strength than a demonstration of precisely applied pressure — the rhino equivalent of using the tip of a chisel instead of the flat of a fist.

CLOSING THE LOOP: WATCHING FUN ONLINE VIDEO WITH SLIGHTLY BETTER EYES

There's a real, practical value in walking away from a clip like this one able to see slightly more than the joke on the surface. The next zoo video that crosses your feed — an elephant using its trunk to solve a puzzle feeder, a big cat pouncing on a frozen treat, an octopus prying open a jar — is very likely the exact same layered thing this rhino clip turned out to be: genuine, well-studied animal anatomy, doing genuine, evolutionarily sensible work, deliberately staged by professional keepers as both welfare enrichment and public education, filmed specifically because it happens to also be extremely fun to watch. None of those layers cancel each other out. The rhino wasn't performing for the camera, and the zoo wasn't lying about the enrichment purpose, and the audience wasn't wrong to laugh — all three things are simultaneously, completely true, and that layered honesty is precisely what separates a good piece of zoo content from a hollow one.

THE SMALL DETAIL WORTH REMEMBERING

Next time a clip like this crosses your feed, the single fact worth actually holding onto is the one most people never learn: that horn is hair. Dense, ancient, evolutionarily refined hair, built by the same biological machinery that grows your own fingernails, shaped by millions of years of natural selection into a tool precise enough to split a watermelon clean down the middle and gentle enough, in the same motion, to leave the animal wielding it completely unharmed. It's one of the more elegant pieces of engineering in the entire animal kingdom, currently being hunted nearly to extinction for a superstition with no basis in what that horn is actually made of — and, for one satisfying, sticky, sixteen-second stretch of video, doing exactly what it evolved to do: getting an animal fed.

And that, more than the crack or the crunch or the juice sprayed across the gravel, is the actual headline hiding inside sixteen seconds of a rhino demolishing a watermelon: a species still recovering from near-catastrophe, represented by one very healthy, very well-fed individual, using precisely the tool everyone keeps getting wrong about, to do precisely the thing that tool was built for all along.

text:
Sorry I should have said no good harbors

A “harbour” needs more than an indentation in the coastline. To support a major city it ideally needs:

A protected entrance usable in bad weather
Deep water requiring limited dredging
Enough sheltered space for docks and ships
Good connections to a large inland economy

The outer Washington–Oregon coast rarely offers all four.

Grays Harbor — Aberdeen and Hoquiam

Grays Harbor is a shallow estuary with sediment, tidal flats and a bar at its entrance. Maintaining a reliable shipping channel requires dredging. Aberdeen therefore became a significant timber town, but not a natural rival to Seattle.

Willapa Bay — near Long Beach

Willapa Bay is enormous, but much of it is shallow mudflat and oyster habitat. 

The Columbia River — Astoria

This is the most consequential opening on the outer coast, but the Columbia Bar is famously treacherous. River sediment meets Pacific waves and currents, producing shifting shoals and rough water. Astoria sits near the entrance, but the river provided access to better port locations farther inland. Portland’s calmer location, rail connections and access to the Willamette Valley outweighed the extra river journey.

Oregon coast

Tillamook Bay

Protected but shallow, sediment-prone and reached through a difficult entrance. It serves fishing and recreation, not deep-draft international shipping.

Yaquina Bay — Newport

One of the better central-coast harbours, protected by jetties and used by fishing vessels and research ships. But it is relatively small, its entrance and channel require engineering, and the Coast Range separates it from Oregon’s population and industry.

Coos Bay

Probably the strongest candidate for a major outer-coast port. It has a reasonably large estuary and historically shipped timber. But the entrance must be dredged and stabilized, the surrounding region is relatively remote, and transportation links across the mountains are weak. Once the timber industry declined, there was not enough other traffic to generate metropolitan growth.

Brookings and Yachats

These have little or no major natural harbour. Brookings has an engineered small-craft harbour at the mouth of the Chetco River; Yachats essentially has an exposed rocky coastline. Cannon Beach has no protected port at all.

text:
‘It’s a deportation mill’ – Immigration lawyer admits total defeat in Trump’s America… | BellaVita, Revolver News

Sometimes the best advertisement for a policy comes from the people who absolutely hate it.

Meet Karla Navarrete.

She’s a California immigration attorney whose business is apparently booming under President Trump.

But it’s not booming because immigrants suddenly discovered an exciting new venture. It’s booming because Trump is doing exactly what he spent years promising Americans he would do… he’s enforcing immigration law and removing people who don’t have a legal right to be here.

Yes, this is what we voted for, but Navarrete isn’t celebrating.

She’s downright miserable and feels totally defeated in Trump’s America.

Again, we voted for this.

She says she now spends six days a week dealing with clients whose chances of remaining in America are pretty much donezo. Her small operation has blown up in a big way, and the criminals coming through her doors are now hearing an answer they hoped they’d never hear…

Sorry, but you have to go home.

Of course, the LA Times sympathetic version of this story focuses entirely on how painful that is for the criminals breaking our laws.

Now, we’ll acknowledge that some stories are sad. After all, many of these criminals dragged their poor children here. They built their lives around the fantasy that Biden’s gravy train would keep on flowing.

So, yes, when the law finally caught up, it reality hit hard.

But there’s another side of this story that deserves more than just misplaced sadness.

Trump didn’t sneak this policy into Washington after the election. He campaigned on closing the border and sending the criminals back home.

Illegal immigration and the chaos at the southern border were huge issues during the 2024 election. Americans voted for this.

Now that enforcement is actually happening, the same elites and media who spent years treating the border like a “welcome mat” want Americans to believe actually enforcing the rules is evil. Maybe the bigger scandal was convincing millions of people that those rules would never be enforced in the first place.

Because Navarrete knows that the criminals stumbling into her office don’t have a strong legal case to stay.

The LA Times piece opens by describing a poor, downtrodden lawyer whose practice has turned into a chaotic mess, while her optimism for her clients has hit an all-time low.

Business is better than ever for Karla Navarrete. And she’s not happy about it at all.

She’s an immigration attorney who spends six days a week telling people that they have little chance of staying in Donald Trump’s America.

“It’s become a deportation mill, and my clients have been placed on speeding rockets,” Navarrete, the daughter of a Mexican immigrant, told me at her South Gate office around 8 on a recent Monday morning.

The 42-year-old mother of four had arrived at sunrise to prep for a day of virtual and in-person court hearings and free walk-in consultations. Tchotchkes gifted by grateful clients prettied the pink cabinets and pink walls. Amid statues and posters of the Virgen de Guadalupe was a rosary that a man had made of hardened bread during his months in an immigration detention facility.

On Navarrete’s desk were two Mac laptops and another computer, all logged into immigration courts across the Southland. The private practice she started in 2022 in a small suite now occupies an entire floor and a downstairs reception area, with satellite offices in Chino and downtown Los Angeles.

“Almost none of my clients have a winning case based on current law,” she continued. “’¿Si pasan reforma? [If they pass immigration reform?]’ is their most favorite question. But it’s not just Trump. It’s Stephen Miller, it’s Congress, and it’s becoming the courts.”

That last admission does a ton of heavy lifting, right?

“Almost none of my clients have a winning case based on current law.”

Well, there you go… the law actually works, as long as you apply it. Who knew?

Trump didn’t wake up one morning and decide to be mean to immigrants. He woke up and decided to enforce the laws on the books.

And her little testimony explains why her cases are colliding with the law.

Just because Washington allowed an enormous gap to grow between immigration laws and immigration policy doesn’t mean enforcement is evil. What’s actually evil is left-wing politicians and media props encouraging people to make a dangerous trek to break the law.

Thankfully, Trump is closing the gap.

And yes, maybe that’ll feel harsh to people who built their entire career and future around the old, failed system. But just because a law was unenforced doesn’t magically make it not a law.

And the scale of what’s happening inside Navarrete’s office shows just how dramatically things have changed.

Now, her clients are giving up and choosing to leave.

LA Times:

Navarrete’s life changed last June when she got a phone call while hanging out with her preteen daughter.

Immigration agents had staged a mass raid of Ambiance Apparel in L.A.’s Fashion District. She headed over, finding that friends from UCLA, Loyola Law School and her time working for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights were converging there.

“We were like, ‘What are we going to do? Is this really happening? This, in L.A.?’” she said.

It was the start of a summer of raids that soon went nationwide and have never really ended.

At the time, most of Navarrete’s clients were women applying for a U visa, which offers legal status for crime victims who assist law enforcement in the prosecution of perpetrators. She quickly transitioned to helping people caught up in Trump’s deportation deluge, earning clients through word of mouth as well as through nonprofits such as the CLEAN Carwash Worker Center, which organizes carwasheros across Southern California.

Most of her clients now are middle-aged men, who often choose deportation over the harsh reality of staying in immigration detention indefinitely.

“It’s the younger ones who want to wait it out longer,” she said on the drive down to Santa Ana. An assistant took the wheel of Navarrete’s Range Rover so her boss could catch up on emails, calls and texts.

The mainstream media job these days is to only focus on the criminal being deported.

But immigration policy doesn’t start or stop with the people sneaking over.

It affects American wages, housing, schools, and public services, and perhaps most importantly, it affects hardworking Americans competing for work in industries that favor cheap, inexperienced illegal labor.

Which brings us to a perspective you should see more of…

An American contractor explaining what Trump’s deportation has done for his and others’ livelihoods.

That’s the American human story that matters.

For every mainstream article sobbing over an illegal facing deportation, there are American workers trying to make rent, raise children, win contracts, and earn a decent living, and they can’t, thanks to illegal immigration.

And nobody from the press follows them around for fourteen hours asking how immigration policy changed their lives.

But when an American contractor tells you the people in his industry suddenly have a helluva lot more work, maybe the press outta listen.

The media, and Navarrete’s dismay and frustration at the tide turning, are palatable, and you can see clearly why the left hates ICE so much. Law enforcement goes against everything they stand for, which is scary.

LA Times:

Around 9 p.m., Navarrete let out a sigh. Another 14-hour day was about to end. She picked up her personal phone to check on her family and grabbed a bag for back-to-school supplies she had ordered from Amazon.

“It was hard today,” Navarrete said. “It was a lot of bad news. No one was a straight shot.”

I asked why she was so blunt with people about their chances.

“I can’t tell them it’s going to be OK. I don’t want to lie: It’s never been this bad,” she said. “I used to call my presentations ‘Know Your Rights’ workshops. Now, they’re just workshops, because there are no rights.”

Navarrete pulled out new V-neck law firm T-shirts for her employees, made by a grateful client.

“As crazy and as chaotic as it can get, every once in awhile, you get a win,” she continued. “And that’s what makes it all worthwhile. It’s gotten harder but more gratifying, because I always wanted to go against ICE, the arch-nemesis of my life.”

Having a bad immigration case isn’t the same thing as having no rights… what an absurd thing to suggest.

The cruelest part of this whole mess happened years earlier, when politicians and activists encouraged people to believe America’s immigration laws were “optional” and invited them over.

That promise was never theirs to make.

Now Trump is enforcing rules that were sitting on the books all along, and suddenly the immigration lawyers are busier and sadder than ever.

But the real story here isn’t about the criminal. It’s about the American workers who are looking around and discovering something very different….

More opportunity.

And yes, we absolutely voted for this.

text:
Exercise for Fun May Protect the Brain | Knowridge

Being physically active is widely considered one of the best habits for healthy aging.

But a major new study suggests that where and why people are active may be just as important as how much they move.

Researchers found that exercise done during free time was linked to a substantially lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, physical activity performed as part of a demanding job was linked to a higher risk.

The study was led by researchers at the University of Southern California, or USC. It brought together evidence involving more than 4.2 million people, making it one of the largest investigations of physical activity and dementia.

Dementia is a general term for serious problems with memory, thinking and everyday abilities. Alzheimer’s disease is its most common form, while vascular dementia is caused by problems with blood flow to the brain.

Previous research has repeatedly found that exercise can support brain health. Physical activity can improve blood flow, support heart health and help control conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes, which are themselves linked to dementia.

But many earlier studies treated all physical activity as if it were the same. A morning walk, a game of tennis, lifting heavy objects at work and standing for hours during a shift could all be counted as physical activity.

The USC researchers wanted to know whether that approach was hiding important differences. They examined 74 previous studies involving people between 45 and 93 years old from 30 countries.

Participants were followed for a typical period of about 10 years. Researchers tracked cases of dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.

The results showed a striking difference between exercise during free time and activity at work. People with higher levels of leisure-time physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with those who were least active.

Leisure exercise included activities such as walking, cycling, swimming, running and playing sports. The apparent benefit increased as people became more active before eventually leveling off.

The pattern was very different for physical activity at work. People with higher levels of job-related physical activity had a 20% higher risk of dementia.

At first, this may sound strange. If movement is healthy, why wouldn’t a physically demanding job provide the same benefits as walking or swimming after work?

Researchers say the answer may lie in the conditions surrounding the activity rather than the movement itself. Leisure exercise is usually voluntary and can often be adjusted according to how a person feels.

People can slow down when they become tired, take breaks and choose activities they enjoy. Exercise can also involve spending time outdoors, meeting friends and reducing stress.

Physical work can be very different. A worker may spend hours lifting, standing, bending or repeating the same movements without having much control over the pace.

People in manual jobs may also face greater workplace stress, noise, air pollution or other harmful exposures. They may have fewer opportunities to recover properly between periods of physical effort.

Fatigue may create another problem. Someone who spends an entire day doing demanding physical work may understandably have little energy left for recreational exercise afterward.

Scientists have seen a similar pattern in heart research. It is sometimes called the “physical activity paradox,” in which leisure exercise is associated with better health while high levels of occupational activity do not provide the same protection.

The new study suggests this paradox may also apply to dementia. However, the researchers stressed that their findings do not prove that physical work causes dementia.

Most of the studies were observational, meaning researchers watched what happened in people’s lives rather than assigning them to different kinds of activity. Other differences between people in manual and less physically demanding jobs could therefore help explain the results.

Education, income, workplace conditions, access to health care and other social factors may all influence dementia risk. Although researchers tried to account for several differences, it is impossible to remove every possible influence.

There were other limitations. Most studies depended on people remembering and reporting how active they were, and much of the evidence came from wealthier countries.

There was also too little research on housework and active commuting to reach strong conclusions. Household activity appeared beneficial, while active commuting showed a small increase in risk, but those findings were based on very few studies.

Overall, the research should not be interpreted as a warning against physical jobs. Instead, it challenges the simple idea that every form of movement produces exactly the same health effects.

The most convincing finding is the continued benefit associated with voluntary exercise during leisure time. Creating opportunities for people to walk, swim, cycle, play sports or enjoy other activities may therefore be particularly important for healthy aging.

The study was led by Professor David Raichlen and first author Natan Feter of USC and was published in The Lancet Public Health. The huge number of participants strengthens the findings, but because the evidence is observational, the results show an association rather than direct cause and effect.

The study offers an important change in how we think about exercise and brain health. Movement matters, but enjoyable activity with enough rest and personal control may be very different from spending long hours doing repetitive or stressful physical work.

It’s also worth noting that the Coliseum is the largest-capacity stadium in the City of LA. For the less exciting matchups, there are plenty of ways to make games feel like events: Homecoming, rivalry weekends, alumni events, giveaways, collectibles, special promotions, and family packages. And when they come, they’ll enjoy visiting the new Lucas Museum and the Science Center’s new space shuttle exhibit while they’re there. LA indeed has a lot to offer.
